#1251. Most expensive goal in Liverpool history gives Iraola era lift-off

A quick sprint, a well-placed pass and an instinctive finish. Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak will have done this dozens of times in training but here, on a squally Sunday afternoon, this combination secured a little piece of history.

Anfield has witnessed plenty of significant goals down the years but never had this crowd seen one that cost £248m to make. Liverpool invested a near quarter-billion pounds on Barcola and Isak for bigger occasions than a tussle with Brighton and Hove Albion, but this rapid interchange felt like a significant moment.

Liverpool are a work in progress under Andoni Iraola but with each minute of each game you can see signs of things knitting together, and if Barcola and Isak are finding harmony, with Florian Wirtz in behind, then, perhaps, this journey will start to accelerate.

This was an important afternoon for Liverpool’s head coach, a difficult assignment against high-flying, well-respected opponents in Brighton, who arrived on Merseyside having won their last four Premier League fixtures with a combined aggregate of 15-0, including a 3-0 thumping of reigning champions Arsenal.

But Liverpool rose impressively to the challenge and there are grounds for saying this was the most significant success to date for Iraola, whose team defended relentlessly to preserve a clean sheet. They are up to fourth now after this 2-0 success and deserve their position.

“I’m very happy,” Iraola said. “We faced a very good opponent, similar to Villarreal [in the Champions League]. It’s difficult to defend them a lot of times and it was key how we started. We needed to be aggressive, recover balls, win our duels, be dangerous in transitions: I think we’ve done it.”

And how. Iraola was able to march towards the Kop at the end, to clap the supporters and acknowledge only Liverpool’s fifth (and his first) Premier League win at Anfield in 2026, and it was evident he had a spring in his step from what he had seen.

Whether the game would have flowed in the direction it did had Brighton taken the lead can only be speculated but what a glorious chance they wasted for us to find out: in the 13th minute, five swift, one-touch passes bamboozled Liverpool’s defence and created space for Yasin Ayari.

With the goal at his mercy, Ayari could have made things exceptionally uncomfortable but he leant back and blazed over. He clasped his face and grimaced, knowing what had gone begging in front of the Kop; four minutes later, his misery was exacerbated.

"He's GOT to hit the target!" Yasin Ayari missed a golden chance to put Brighton ahead against Liverpool 🫣 https://t.co/Qz7G3sXCpP

Liverpool’s lead was secured with an element of good fortune but, equally, the tenacity of Ronald Araújo and Wirtz was instrumental in pressing Brighton back to the point that they were panicking; Wirtz’s shot, deflected off Pascal Gross past Bart Verbruggen, compounded it all.

“I think everyone in the stadium – and you as well – felt there was a missed opportunity for us,” groaned Fabian Hürzeler, the visitors’ head coach. “It’s not only after the goal or the goals they scored. Before they scored, we had two big chances. I think it was just the difference that they scored and we didn’t score.”

It would be wrong to say Wirtz was doing cartwheels – perhaps he knew immediately he would not get the goal – but it was an important moment for him and you could feel the sense of goodwill towards him from team-mates and supporters alike.

Florian Wirtz's deflected shot has put Liverpool ahead minutes after Brighton had a great chance of their own ⚽️ https://t.co/b6mRvl2rSR

Remarkably, this was the first time Liverpool had scored in the first half at Anfield in a Premier League fixture since May 9 and, with that momentum, it led to one of those periods when they started attacking in waves and carried the crowd with them.

What they needed was a second goal to arrive quite quickly and that is what happened when Barcola won possession, scuttled forward and played a perfectly weighted bobbling ball into Isak’s path; the Swede did the rest, calmly finishing from eight yards.

Everything with Isak feels to be going under the radar at the moment, but that is six goals in six Premier League appearances. He is starting to show the consistency and killer instinct that everyone felt he would. Iraola will be hoping it continues for the foreseeable future.

Alexander Isak scores to double Liverpool's lead at Anfield! 💥 https://t.co/oYs2jnHZEb

“The performance was really good,” said Isak, the quiet assassin. “We were really solid against a really good team. The first half is what we really want to be about. It was about intensity, winning balls and countering.”

Brighton, as much as Hürzeler protested, could not properly recover, though this is no criticism. They remain committed to attack, they struck the frame of the goal when Ayari tried to punish an Alisson Becker mistake and the desire to keep pushing ensured Liverpool could never relax.

What Liverpool had going for them this time, however, was an intensity to preserve a clean sheet and nobody embodied the indefatigability more than Araújo, the Uruguay international whose loan from Barcelona is looking an increasingly shrewd piece of business.

Two moments stood out: one thunderous tackle on substitute Malick Yalcouyé in front of the Main Stand that had the locals roaring their approval, another in the first half when he was on the floor but still managed to head away to thwart Maxim De Cuyper.

They remember those moments as much as the stardust that Barcola and Isak provide. Put it all together and it might just be a launchpad for Iraola.

"The performance was really solid" Alexander Isak reacts after scoring in Liverpool's win against Brighton 🗣️ https://t.co/Zei2tmWVix

Iraola has his first Premier League home win in charge of Liverpool thanks to a 2-0 victory over Brighton. The hosts netted twice in the first half through Wirtz’s deflected strike off Gross and Isak’s close-range finish. This result moves Liverpool above Chelsea and up to fourth, just a point behind third-place Brighton, who suffer their first defeat in any competition since August 30.

Three points at Anfield 😍 #LIVBHA https://t.co/AnAlNgOzlu

Still, Brighton can’t find a way through Liverpool’s resilient defence. Araujo’s well-time sliding challenge on Kostoulas draws huge cheers from the home fans.

Ronald Araujo has become a cult figure very quickly and he’s just provided the moment of the second half with a challenge that was a well received by those in the Main Stand as a goal. Liverpool are working relentlessly to preserve their clean sheet and Andoni Iraola is imploring his players to retain their focus until the end.

There will be four minutes of added time. Brighton need a goal as soon as possible. Liverpool are closing in on an impressive win.

So wasteful from Brighton... They have a great chance to put the ball into the box with a free kick, but De Cuyper wastefully launches it out of play. With Gross also stood over it, you expected him take it. Liverpool then make a late change as Tsimikas replaces Kerkez for the final few minutes.

Gakpo drives forward and smashes a wild long-range shot wide. His end-product has been lacking today, but he’s undoubtedly caused Brighton problems with his dribbling, movement and directness.

A spell of Brighton pressure ends as Rutter can’t quite find Kostoulas with a low cross. The young striker stays down and replays show that Jacquet stood on his foot as the defender attempted a clearance. However, it’s quickly checked and cleared by VAR. There wasn’t much in the challenge at all.

Kerkez scampers into Brighton’s box, reaching the byline, but he can’t dig out a cross as the chance disappears. Brighton will need to throw everything forward soon.

Now, that double change from Liverpool is here. Barcola and Isak depart to large applause, with Ngumoha and Koumas cheered on as they run onto the pitch.

As expected, Rutter is on. He replaces Ayari, who will think back to his missed chance and shot off the post in the first half.

Gakpo brilliantly turns Costinha, who pulls the winger back to deservedly pick up a booking. Both sides look to be readying changes, with Ngumoha, Koumas and Rutter poised to enter the action.

Brighton seem to have hit a wall in this second half. They’ve struggled to create chances since the break. Liverpool are working really hard defensively.

Once again, Liverpool break through Gakpo. This time, it comes from a Brighton corner, but Gakpo’s cross for Isak at the back post is read by Dunk.

In his first involvement since entering the action, Nyoni ends a slick Brighton move by taking the ball off De Cuyper’s toe in the penalty area with a much-needed clearance. He seems to be limping after he was caught by De Cuyper.

Wirtz’s game is over and he departs to be replaced by Nyoni in Liverpool’s first change.

After some treatment for Wirtz, Vuskovic eventually takes the free kick. It’s in such an inviting position, but the defender gets too power on his strike and whips it over the bar.

This game is still very much in the balance, even though Liverpool have a two goal advantage, and it speaks volumes about both teams’ commitment to attack. The questions the respective head coaches are asking of their players are relentless but the players are responding by being adventurous in how they attack and where they want to get on the ball. How Andoni Iraola and Fabian Hurzeler deploy their substitutes will be significant.

Liverpool are holding firm, with Brighton yet to create an opportunity in this second half. Ayari is apprehended by Wirtz to win a free kick on the edge of the area. Despite committing the foul, Wirtz has stayed down and is clutching his ankle.

Brighton make another change and it’s a straight swap in midfield as Yalcouye replaces Chema Andres, who hobbles off the pitch.

With Brighton requiring at least two goals to avoid defeat, they’ll need to push a lot of men forward, which will open up space for Liverpool to exploit on the break. If there is one, the next goal in this game is crucial.

Liverpool break through Gakpo, who sprints from inside his own half into the penalty. He tries to release Isak, but his pass is intercepted by Vuskovic as he’s swarmed by the Brighton defence. Gakpo waited too long and should have played the pass earlier.

Kerkez isn’t switched on and fails to deal with a long ball, allowing Gomez to race in behind. Van Dijk covers Kerkez and blocks Gomez’s pass, with Kostoulas sprinting up in support.

We are back under way for the second half. Hurzeler has made one half-time alteration, with Hinshelwood replacing Boscagli, who was booked just before the break. Meanwhile, Liverpool are unchanged as they look to protect their two-goal advantage.

Wirtz’s wickedly deflected strike off Gross and Isak’s neat finish from close range mean Liverpool are two goals in front against Brighton. The visitors have also looked dangerous going forward, with Ayari wasting a golden chance when the score was still goalless, before hitting the post in the 36th minute. As it stands, this result would move Liverpool into fourth and a point behind Brighton, who need a massive second-half performance.

Two goals to the good for @LFC 😮‍💨 A Pascal Gross own goal puts the Reds ahead, before Alexander Isak fires in the second 🔴 https://t.co/AglQOyUIoY

Brighton are desperate to find a goal before the break as Kostoulas’ fierce shot is batted away by Alisson, whose goal is living a charmed life. Boscagli then receives a yellow card for blocking Barcola’s off-the-ball run.

No getting away from the fact that Brighton simply haven’t got started and it’s a huge surprise. What chances they have had came from Liverpool’s own shortcomings and it is impossible to think they will be so off the pace in the second period. Fabian Hurzeler has remained composed, which is more than can be said for Oliver Boscagli, who looks like he is playing pass the parcel, so anxious is he to get rid of the ball - often with a mistake.

On the counter, Gomez tries to find Ayari with a pass, but Jacquet’s touch knocks the ball out of Liverpool’s box. There will be three minutes of added time to end this half.

Araujo forces a save as he sprints forward from his right-back position to receive a clipped pass from Mac Allister, before shooting from a tight angle to sting the palms of Verbruggen with a drilled effort.

Gakpo drives at Brighton’s defence and then nearly squeezes a low cross to the supporting Isak, but Dunk’s crucial intervention with his outstretched leg prevents a chance.

Off the post for Brighton. Ayari shoots from an incredibly long way out as Brighton dispossess Mac Allister and Jacquet, however his curling effort agonisingly bounces against the post and out, with Alisson well beaten.

Despite falling two goals behind in this first half, Brighton have recorded 83% possession over the previous five minutes.

There’s a small confrontation between Vuskovic and Gakpo, which is quickly checked and cleared by VAR. In the next passage of play, Kerkez tees up Gakpo, who bursts into the box and reaches the byline, but his cross is blocked by Dunk.

A smooth Brighton move ends with Jacquet making a crucial block to deny Kostoulas from close range. Liverpool eventually scramble it clear. That’s a reminder of the threat that Brighton can pose.

Brighton look stunned. Since Ayari missed that chance, they’ve been swarmed by Liverpool, whose forwards are in the mood for some goals today.

Two goals in quick succession propel Liverpool into a commanding lead. So much credit must go to Barcola. He closes down Boscagli, beats the defender to the loose ball with his blistering pace and then delivers a pinpoint cross towards Isak, who gets across his marker at the near post to direct a first-time finish into the far bottom corner.

Alexander Isak scores to double Liverpool's lead at Anfield! 💥 https://t.co/oYs2jnHZEb

Gakpo bursts in behind Brighton’s defence and outpaces Vuskovic. From a tight angle, the winger shoots, forcing Verbruggen into a decent save. Liverpool are looking very slick in forward areas.

Brighton pay for that missed opportunity at the other end. Araujo’s cross isn’t properly cleared and the ball falls to Wirtz, whose driven effort takes a deflection off Gross and spins into the bottom corner. It’s been awarded as an own-goal. Just a couple of minutes earlier, Ayari should have put Brighton ahead. Instead, they find themselves a goal behind.

Florian Wirtz's deflected shot has put Liverpool ahead minutes after Brighton had a great chance of their own ⚽️ https://t.co/b6mRvl2rSR

Florian Wirtz is taking the acclaim but that looks very much like it will be a Pascal Gross own goal. Whether it is credited to him or not, his strength to win possession and keep Liverpool on the front foot was hugely important. You wouldn’t say he is beaming from ear to ear but let’s see how he is at the final whistle. The first goal in this contest had the potential to be hugely important.

Brighton miss a golden chance. Gomez threads a delightful ball past Van Dijk through to Gross, who unselfishly squares it to Ayari. However, the Sweden international sweeps a first-time effort over the bar with the goal gaping. Brighton should be ahead.

"He's GOT to hit the target!" Yasin Ayari missed a golden chance to put Brighton ahead against Liverpool 🫣 https://t.co/Qz7G3sXCpP

Barcola tries to race onto a loose ball, but Verbruggen rushes out of his box to beat the pacey winger to it.

Liverpool’s fast start continues as Wirtz curls an exquisite pass from a wide position around Brighton’s defence for Isak to latch onto. The striker can’t take the ball in his stride, allowing Vuskovic to clear. Gakpo then bends a whipped effort into Verbruggen’s arms.

Brighton are currently playing with 10 men due to Kadioglu’s absence as Liverpool apply some pressure. The visitors eventually clear Wirtz’s searching cross. Confirmation of that change sees Costinha replace Kadioglu in Brighton’s backline.

There’s an early issue for Brighton’s Kadioglu, who is sit on the deck clutching his hip. He bumped into Wirtz and Gravenberch in quick succession as he attempted to win the ball. Hurzeler could be forced into a change here.

We are under way at Anfield. Can Iraola get his first home league win as Liverpool boss or will high-flying Brighton continue to upset the odds and close the gap on Manchester City and Arsenal at the top?

Captains Van Dijk and Dunk lead their respective sides out onto the Anfield pitch in windy conditions. Brighton are four points ahead and two places above Liverpool in the league table. Does that make Liverpool the underdogs in their own back yard?

"We respect the opposition, they are doing amazing" Andoni Iraola speaks ahead of Liverpool vs Brighton 🗣️ https://t.co/YRYJong4xD

"We come here believing." 👊💬 https://t.co/M0M0R3MZxe

Welcome to Anfield, where we have just had four seasons in 10 minutes: rain was overtaken by sunshine, all the while the wind has been blowing past itself, the kind that wouldn’t just turn an umbrella inside out but carry you off into the distance. Racing was abandoned at Aintree, which is just two miles away, early this morning but there have been no such worries at Anfield. The pitch is actually well sheltered from the elements, so hopefully it won’t impact on the game too much. These sides both want to play football and we can safely say (famous last words) that it won’t be 0-0 at 90 minutes.

Even by his prodigious standards, this has been a different week for Rio Ngumoha. After the coming-of-age performance against Villarreal, so followed the slew of attention on social media.

A clip of his best moments during the chaotic 4-3 dispatching of the Spaniards, posted on Uefa’s official X account, attracted 1.2 million views and was liked more than 24,000 times. Hot on the heels came another video, this time when he was 11, when he nutmegged a dumbfounded cameraman.

Ngumoha has always had feet that move as quickly as the hands of street artists who perform tricks with cups and balls: now you see it, now you don’t. We live in an age where talent is quickly amplified and this young England international has it in bundles.

You saw it in those exhilarating 74 minutes: Ngumoha had his most touches in a game this campaign (51), most touches in the opposition box (12) and attempted the most dribbles (10), as well as creating the most chances (three) and providing two assists.

It is the first time an 18-year-old has produced such figures in the Champions League since Opta’s European records began in 2008-09.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League encounter between Liverpool and Brighton & Hove Albion at Anfield.

Liverpool are on a three-game winning run in all competitions, and came from two goals behind in their previous outing in the Champions League on Tuesday, earning an enthralling 4-3 victory over Villarreal. Last weekend, Andoni Iraola’s men also initially fell behind against Brentford in the Premier League, but netted two second-half goals through Daniel Munoz and Alexander Isak to win 2-1 as their opponents finished with nine men.

In his programme notes, Liverpool boss Iraola was excited about the prospect of a second game in a week at home. “As someone who believes every single opportunity we have to play a game at this stadium and in front of our supporters is a privilege, I also feel very passionately that this is a period that we should continue to embrace,” he said.

“It is also a spell in which we will carry on being tested because the quality of the opposition dictates that there is no chance of anything else. Villarreal pushed us all the way in midweek and everything about the way Brighton have played so far this season tells us that it would be foolish to expect anything but the same today.”

Brighton have emerged as one of the surprise packages of the Premier League season thanks to their blistering start. Fabian Hurzeler’s side sit third in the table, having scored a whopping 23 goals in their opening seven games, while conceding just five. On Thursday, Brighton were unexpectedly held to a 0-0 draw by Czech outfit Jablonec, ending a run of six straight victories in all competitions. Nevertheless, they’re unbeaten since their 4-3 league loss to Chelsea back on August 30.

Defender Ferdi Kadioglu believes his team’s energy and fitness has played a huge role in their eye-catching form. “If you want to play how we play, you have to be very fit,” he said. “We were already fit last season, but I think it’s more that now everyone really understands what we need to do to win matches. That’s really clear this season, and everyone is doing it. Everyone is really focused on their task and doing it very well so far.”

Kick-off is at 14:00, with team news following shortly.

#1250. Allegri: ‘Napoli have limitations, these mistakes cost you matches’

Max Allegri admits Napoli have ‘limitations’ after a 4-1 defeat to FC Porto, as their Champions League campaign hangs by a thread. ‘These are the mistakes that cost you matches.’

The Partenopei were truly decimated going into the Estadio do Dragao, as they were missing 10 players between injuries and ineligibility, leaving only three senior outfield figures on the bench.

In the circumstances, they still got to half-time with the score at 1-1, Scott McTominay cancelling out the free header from Jan Bednarek.

However, they crumbled in the final 20 minutes with a Gabriel Veiga counter-attack, identical Jakub Kiwior header on a corner, and Samu’s penalty after a Rafa Marin red card offence.

“We made mistakes on two set plays, the team had in my view a good performance up to the 70th minute,” Allegri told Sky Sport Italia.

“It was an aggressive performance, we went man for man, but then conceded this second goal on a bouncing ball and with fatigue we didn’t push up in time for the offside.

“These are errors that unfortunately can happen when you are tired. The tempo is high in the Champions League, and in those final minutes we were struggling, as they hit the crossbar twice just before the goal and were cutting through us fairly easily.”

Allegri is now under serious pressure after a series of defeats in big games, and they lost three of the first four Champions League fixtures, so can he turn this around?

“We have a game on Sunday against Lazio and need to recuperate, because these are the only players we’ve got,” he replied.

“You win and lose matches on details, not the big things, but the small ones. The team fought and chased Porto around man for man as long as they could, but then we ran out of fuel.

“It’s like a Cup Final for us against Lazio and then hopefully we can recover some players during the break for international duty.”

This is going to be an extremely tough campaign for Allegri and Napoli, who are falling behind in Serie A and in Europe.

“I had a similar season at Juventus, I’ve been through this before, the only thing we must do is keep working, fix a few things, have that extra metre and extra bit of concentration in certain moments.

“This evening was a better performance than the one we saw on Sunday in Turin, certainly.”

Due to the vast shortage of players, Allegri changed his system to a 3-5-1-1 with Kevin De Bruyne in support of Rasmus Hojlund upfront, so is this the way forward or is it just an emergency?

“I decided to play this way tonight because it was the only way. It went well for over an hour, but Porto made five substitutions, they had fresh legs, and we didn’t have anyone left to introduce.

“If you want to play this way, aggressive and high press, you need to have fresh legs off the bench. It’s either that or you defend in front of your penalty area, but we struggle to do that, so it was the only way.

“Unfortunately, we conceded the second goal on our own clearance.”

Porto lead once again against Napoli 👏 Gabriel Veiga with a smooth finish 🎯 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/g6eg4MXtQ8

— Football on TNT Sports (@footballontnt) November 4, 2026

Sky Sport Italia pundit Fabio Capello asked Allegri if there was anyone who could lead the Napoli defence when they were so visibly disorganised.

“You are perfectly right, but if you look at the bounce of the ball, Beukema just pushed up straight, but when the ball is bouncing around, then he has to mark the man. It was a distraction, he might’ve been tired, but these are details and it was the same thing in Turin.

“There too, there seemed to be no sign of danger, but then we made a mistake, that time it was Marianucci who turned the wrong way. These are mistakes that make you lose games,” replied the Napoli coach.

Allegri then seemed to suggest this was not just down to the current injury crisis, but rather his lack of faith in the side.

“I know the limitations of this squad. In the first game with Genoa, I was accused of having a bad first half, but it was because we needed to control the tempo. Lately, we’ve had good first halves, but then fall away in the second half, it’s because we have a limited squad.

“If the same lot play every three days, the tempo is high, by the 70th minute it becomes a different match. You can only control that if you have eight or nine players on the bench. Now we’ve got one more game to play with Lazio, then we’ll see what happens when more return.”

#1249. Politano: ‘Napoli cannot have this attitude, only Italians take responsibility’

Matteo Politano seemed to launch a broadside at his Napoli teammates after the 4-1 defeat to FC Porto, noting it was ‘just us Italians’ who took responsibility for their difficulties.

The Partenopei had started quite strong at the Estadio do Dragao this evening, despite having a decimated squad with 10 players out between injury and ineligibility, leaving only three senior outfield figures on the bench.

The Jan Bednarek header on a corner was cancelled out by Scott McTominay, but they crumbled in the final 20 minutes to Gabriel Veiga’s counter-attack, another free header from Jakub Kiwior and the late Samu penalty with Rafa Marin red card.

When Politano was the first to speak after the match, Sky Sport Italia noted it was ‘always you’ who comes to represent the squad in the media room.

“It would be nice if a few other teammates came here to give an explanation and not just us Italians, but never mind,” replied Politano with what could only be described as a bitter laugh.

Napoli had hoped for better after the 2-0 Serie A defeat to Juventus at the weekend, but have now lost three out of four Champions League matches.

“We didn’t see the progress we wanted. The first half had been a good approach, we had equalised and created a few more chances that we could’ve done better, but we conceded two goals from corners and they hit the crossbar twice, all from the same situations, so there’s not a lot to say there,” added Politano.

“The attitude is one that a team like ours cannot have at this level.”

Considering his comment about only the Italians stepping up, does Politano feel there is a lack of unity at Napoli, or that Max Allegri is losing control of the side?

“I was not attacking anyone, we have a squad that is struggling, but we need to come together and think about this next game before the break for international duty. Hopefully we can recover a few players during that spell and then our season can really begin.”

It is a recurring theme that Napoli tend to crumble in the last 30 minutes of matches, both in Serie A and Europe, so is it purely a physical problem?

“I don’t know, we have asked ourselves that too. At times, it is not even a tactical issue, as we are all behind the ball, but we lack the determination and sharpness, we don’t read situations well or sense danger,” added Politano.

“In the Champions League and Serie A, the moment you leave the slightest bit of space, they punish you.”

Speaking to Amazon Prime Video Italia, Politano also added that “losing 2-1 and losing 4-1 is a big difference. We melted at the second goal and we need to take a good look at ourselves.”

#1248. Valverde played over 40 minutes injured as Real Madrid face three away games in a week

Real Madrid came away from Camp Nou on Sunday night with three points and a new fitness worry. José Mourinho revealed after the 2-1 win over Barcelona that Fede Valverde had spent a large part of the game carrying an injury, and the timing is far from ideal with three away fixtures to come in the space of seven days.

The coach went out of his way to single out the Uruguayan in his post-match press conference, saying Valverde “played injured for more than 40 minutes”. Mourinho added: “He got injured, wanted to continue, pushed himself to his limits, and gave everything while he was on the field.”

Mourinho did not say what kind of injury Valverde had suffered or at what point in the match it happened. At the time of writing, Real Madrid had not published a medical report on the midfielder, who was named in the starting XI alongside Aurélien Tchouaméni, Bernardo Silva and Jude Bellingham.

The club’s English account still made him one of the faces of the night, sharing a Valverde post shortly after midnight.

🗣️ @FedeeValverde 🗣️ pic.twitter.com/iOcHUMmM90

Real Madrid C.F. (@realmadriden) October 26, 2026

Valverde was not the only fitness story of the weekend. Thibaut Courtois dropped out on matchday because of what the club called a flu-like illness, with Illia Voloshyn called up as cover. Andriy Lunin started in goal and, according to Real Madrid’s own match report, made a fine stop from a Gerard Martín header in the 66th minute.

Mourinho said his only message to Lunin before kick-off was simple: “You train to play, not to sit on the bench. Go and play.” He also stressed that the squad had not been rattled by the late change, adding that “today none of us cried before the match because Thibaut wasn’t playing”. Courtois, whose future has been discussed in terms of a possible one-year contract extension, now has a few days to recover before the next game.

The calendar offers Madrid little breathing space. Mourinho pointed out that “on Sunday we play away; then we play away on Wednesday, and then we have another away match on Saturday”. According to the fixture list, those games are against Racing Santander on 1 November, AEK Athens in the Champions League on 4 November and Valencia on 7 November.

That run is where Mourinho’s faith in his squad will be tested. He insisted after the Clásico that “I have a rich bench, with players who can be starters”, and he backed it up at Camp Nou by leaving Eduardo Camavinga among the substitutes days after his strong display in the 4-1 win over RB Leipzig. Camavinga came on and set up the late winner for Kylian Mbappé.

The victory was Madrid’s fifth in a row and, as Mourinho noted, leaves them three points behind Barcelona rather than six or nine. Keeping that momentum through three away games will be far easier with Valverde available, so the club’s next medical update on the midfielder will be closely watched before the trip to Santander.

#1247. An AI-native experimental laboratory for autonomous biomolecular operations

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Developing artificial intelligence (AI)-native experimental laboratories for autonomous scientific exploration with minimal human intervention represents a long-standing goal. Although autonomous experimental systems are emerging1,2,3,4, especially in chemical and materials science, they remain largely confined to domains with singular objectives, well-defined workflows and simple instrumentation. This limitation may reflect an ‘add-on’ architecture that uses AI as a task-specific tool rather than providing it with a global understanding of experiments, especially under engineering-oriented circumstances. Here we present AutoDNA, an AI-native autonomous biomolecular engineering laboratory targeting multi-objective experiments across diverse instruments. Through the co-design of models, experiments and instruments, AutoDNA realizes the co-evolution of AI and the automation system within an end-to-end multi-user framework. The system autonomously orchestrates over 20 types of instruments across more than 11,000 steps to execute core nucleic acid operations including synthesis, transcription, amplification and sequencing, while human intervention is limited to hardware maintenance tasks, such as reagent and labware replenishment. Across four representative applications, AutoDNA matched expert-optimized enzymatic DNA synthesis yields, accelerated concurrent protocol execution by 3.2-fold, completed an end-to-end DNA data storage cycle with exact recovery of the original digital content, and identified and validated a clinically detected KRAS G13D mutation. AutoDNA establishes a blueprint towards science-as-a-service, accelerating biological discovery and advancing various applications in synthetic biology and information storage.

#1246. Chinese brands drop Mbappé as backlash hits LaLiga coverage in China

Kylian Mbappé is facing the biggest commercial crisis of his career in China. Three Chinese companies announced on Tuesday that they are ending their agreements with the Real Madrid forward, and the fallout has already reached LaLiga’s television coverage in one of football’s most valuable markets.

The trigger was a short clip linked to the French online show The Bridge. In it, Mbappé is asked which meme of himself he likes most, and he refers to a video of “a guy … I think he was a Chinese dictator”, before an edited picture of his face on the body of Mao Zedong appears, as reported by the Associated Press. The footage has not been independently verified and, according to the BBC, the show has since taken the original upload off its YouTube channel.

Beverage firm Dongpeng, the dairy group Mengniu and Milkground, which makes cheese, all issued statements on Tuesday in very similar language. None of them spelled out exactly what Mbappé had said, but each referred to hurt national feelings. Dongpeng’s statement, carried by the state-run Global Times, ended with the line: “Effective immediately, we are terminating all cooperation with Kylian Mbappé.”

Mengniu said it “firmly opposes and has zero tolerance for any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people”. Social platform RedNote, whose own content partnership with the player ran out at the end of 2024, said it would take down related promotional material. The Global Times added that Dior, On and Hublot had removed Mbappé content from their Weibo pages, and that new users are currently unable to follow his accounts on RedNote or Weibo.

The row has even reached China’s foreign ministry. Asked about the controversy, a spokesperson said that “words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with joint opposition from all sectors of Chinese society”, according to AP.

The part of the story with the widest reach for Spanish football concerns broadcasting. According to the Global Times, Shanghai outlet The Paper reported that China Media Group, the parent organisation of state broadcaster CCTV, has suspended broadcasts of matches involving LaLiga and Mbappé. CCTV’s news apps have also removed content about the striker. Neither LaLiga nor Real Madrid had commented publicly at the time of writing, and there was no indication of how long any suspension might last.

Mbappé himself has not responded either, and The Bridge has stayed silent. The timing is awkward for player and club alike. Only on Sunday he was on the scoresheet as Madrid won the Clásico 2-1 at Camp Nou, a result that came with its own fitness worries over Fede Valverde.

The “dictator” tag has followed Mbappé for some time, partly because of the influence he is said to hold at club and international level, and he has spoken about it before. In a France Football interview in September he said the memes “sometimes reveals a lack of political and human awareness among people”, as quoted by the BBC.

On the pitch, the forward has been in fine form, with goals and assists in recent weeks including the 4-1 Champions League win over RB Leipzig. Off it, the pressure is now on him to address a backlash that is still growing, with Madrid due at Racing Santander on Sunday.

#1245. Espanyol sack Manolo González hours after 121st-minute Copa exit at Sestao River

Jon Rojo's goal in the last minute of extra time gave Sestao River a 4-3 win and knocked Espanyol out of the Copa del Rey. Within hours the club ended Manolo González's time as head coach, five months after confirming he would stay with Monchi's full backing.

Espanyol dismissed head coach Manolo González on Tuesday 27 October 2026, hours after a 4-3 defeat at Sestao River in the Copa del Rey. Defender Jon Rojo won the round of 128 tie at Estadio Las Llanas from a G. Zorrilla assist. He forced home a loose ball in the box in the 121st minute, just as the tie looked to be heading for penalties, EFE reported.

The match was played in heavy rain that left the Las Llanas pitch almost unplayable. Marcos Fernández put Espanyol ahead from the penalty spot after six minutes. Adri Carrión equalised in the 18th minute and Andoni Ugarte made it 2-1 in the 40th, both goals set up by Eneko Delgado Ginés.

Espanyol levelled with a second penalty in the 90th minute. Gabriel Moscardo then put them 3-2 up in the 96th minute. Ander Laka equalised two minutes later before Rojo’s late winner.

The visitors had 61% of the ball against 39% for Sestao River. Espanyol completed 321 accurate passes to Sestao’s 140. Sestao still managed 9 shots on goal to Espanyol’s 6, and Espanyol goalkeeper Marko Dmitrović made 5 saves to the hosts’ 2. Ugarte was the top-rated player on the night with 8.5.

Before the tie, the team had taken only one point from their previous 15 available in LaLiga, according to AFP. Their last six results in all competitions now read five defeats and one draw, with losses to Racing Santander, Atlético Madrid, Elche and Rayo Vallecano and a 1-1 draw with Málaga.

Sestao River, coached by Ángel Viadero, have gone the other way. The win over Espanyol extended a run of five wins and a draw in their last six matches.

The club’s announcement brought González’s tenure to a close after more than three seasons in charge. He had reached his 100th official match against Sevilla on 7 September. That made him the ninth-longest-serving coach by matches in Espanyol’s history.

Espanyol finished 11th in LaLiga in 2025/26 under González, with 12 wins, 10 draws and 16 defeats. Monchi, the new sporting director, had given him full backing at that stage.

#1244. Urda crash: Copa del Rey ties rescheduled to 13 November, three in international break

The RFEF has spread the 24 Copa del Rey first-round ties postponed after the Urda rail crash across 29 October to 13 November. Valencia, Betis and Celta will now play their ties during the November international break.

A national tragedy has stopped Spanish football. The Royal Spanish Football Federation called off every Copa del Rey first-round tie scheduled for the evening of 28 October. All other matches in competitions it organises were postponed too. The decision was taken out of respect for the victims of the rail crash in Toledo province.

A Renfe high-speed train and an Iryo high-speed train collided near Urda station. The crash killed 68 people and injured 80, Público reported. An investigating judge at the court in Orgaz has ordered the first inquiries into what caused the collision.

The shutdown reached beyond the cup. The federation also postponed the nine first-round matches of the futsal Copa de España. The futsal draw planned for 16:00 on 29 October was cancelled.

Valencia, Betis, Alavés, Celta and Levante were the top-flight clubs due in cup action that evening. Each of them must now squeeze a rearranged tie into its schedule. That extra game has to fit into an already crowded run of league and European fixtures. The timing differs sharply from club to club.

Alavés go first. Regional side Anaitasuna host them at 19:00 on Tuesday 3 November. Levante travel to CD Tarancón two days later, on Thursday 5 November.

Three clubs face a longer wait. Celta close the round away to Salamanca, with kick-off at 21:00 on Friday 13 November. Valencia and Betis are in action earlier that same week. A tie that was meant to be settled in October will now be played while national teams are away.

Mallorca’s tie at CD Alcoyano kicks off at 21:00 on the same Thursday evening, after Levante’s game at Tarancón. COPE’s list of the rearranged ties records Mallorca as a Segunda División side, not a top-flight one.

#1240. Ecological and social cues orchestrate concerted courtship in Drosophila

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Mating decisions are often attributed to the sensory signalling between prospective sexual partners. Yet these interactions are also shaped by the broader environmental context in which they unfold, to appropriately align sexual arousal with reproductive opportunities1,2,3,4,5,6. Here we show that in Drosophila erecta mating is strictly contingent on the ecological and social environment generated as flies densely aggregate in groups on a food patch. We find that food volatiles directly promote male sexual arousal, triggering individuals to sample and pursue potential mates, giving rise to dynamic interactions across the group. The ensuing visual motion transforms each male’s visual field, which in turn further amplifies his arousal, generating a multisensory feedback loop that coordinately promotes courtship across individuals. D. erecta’s strict dependence on environmental cues appears latent in related species, such as Drosophila melanogaster, where food odour can promote arousal7 but is dispensable for vigorous courtship. Comparative circuit analyses show that species-specific thresholds for sexual arousal reflect variation in how olfactory input modulates conserved nodes controlling courtship drive, rendering food volatiles a strict sensory gate only in D. erecta. Together, our findings highlight how environmental cues not directly tied to sexual signalling can profoundly influence reproductive behaviour and reorganize the social landscape to ensure mating occurs in contexts where reproductive opportunities are abundant.

Social cues are essential for coordinating interactions between individuals, facilitating the emergence of group dynamics including mating, aggression and collective foraging8,9,10. Yet social interactions do not occur in isolation. Rather, they unfold in a broader environmental context that structures when, where and how social behaviours are expressed. Courtship and mating, for example, often take place at ecologically privileged locations—food sources1,2, prominent visual landmarks3,4 or suitable nesting sites5,6—where many individuals aggregate, either to increase their encounters with prospective sexual partners or to access key resources that promote reproductive success. In these settings, a central component of the environment is the social collective itself: the multisensory backdrop that emerges from the movement, sensory signals and interactions across all individuals in a group11,12,13,14. Social behaviours are therefore likely shaped by both the static properties of the physical environment and the dynamic features of the social landscape. Yet the neural mechanisms that integrate these distinct sensory streams to regulate social arousal states and structure interindividual interactions remain largely unknown.

The mating behaviours of Drosophila offer a powerful inroad to explore how animals adapt to complex ecological and social landscapes. Species in the Drosophila genus vary widely in their ecology and geographic distribution15,16,17,18,19,20, raising the possibility that mating strategies have evolved in concert with the diverse sensory environments in which reproduction occurs. Many species, including members of the Drosophila melanogaster subgroup, mate on their host plants, typically decaying ephemeral substrates where many individuals congregate17, creating a complex social backdrop for reproduction. Other species reproduce in more isolated social settings. Drosophila elegans, for example, establish individual territories and mate on their host flowers19, whereas species of the Hawaiian subgroup perform competitive lekking in the vegetation surrounding their hosts20. The evolution of Drosophila courtship behaviours may therefore have been shaped by the distinct sensory ecology of a species’ mating site and the structure and dynamics of the social groups that form there.

Reproduction and population density in Drosophila erecta, a close relative of D. melanogaster, are tightly linked to the seasonal availability of its host fruit—the screwpine Pandanus21—creating a narrow window of opportunity for individuals to meet and mate22. Such restricted access raises the possibility that D. erecta has evolved behavioural adaptations that couple reproduction to sensory cues emanating from its host, allowing environmental signals not associated with sexual communication to shape mating behaviour. Here we show that the olfactory volatiles emanating from a food patch exert both direct and indirect control over courtship in D. erecta. We find that food volatiles serve as a potent environmental trigger in this species, driving aggregation and serving as a stringent sensory gate to control a male’s sexual arousal. In parallel, environmental food odours shape the visual landscape in which courtship unfolds by encouraging males to approach and sample prospective mates, amplifying visual motion to transform the sensory backdrop of the social scene. D. erecta males are highly sensitive to this increase in visual motion, in contrast to D. melanogaster, pointing to the evolution of a multisensory feedback loop that coordinates male sexual arousal across members of the group, linking courtship to the broader social context. We show that species-specific differences in the sensitivity to environmental cues seem to arise from variation in how olfactory information impinges on conserved components of the courtship circuitry, indicating a potential neural substrate for the rapid tuning of sensory thresholds that govern sexual arousal. Together, these findings show how both ecological and social cues shape species-specific reproductive strategies. Moreover, our observations underscore that the social landscape forms an integral part of the environment—both reflecting the collective dynamics of the group and actively shaping the sensory experience of each individual in it.

To investigate how environmental factors shape the reproductive decisions of species with different ecological preferences, we compared the dynamics of groups of D. erecta and D. melanogaster (five males and five females) provided with a small patch of agar perfumed with food volatiles (diameter 21.5 mm) at the centre of a large arena (diameter 190 mm), a configuration intended to mimic the presence of a localized feeding site (Fig. 1a). Although D. erecta and D. melanogaster have distinct hosts and divergent olfactory preferences16,23, both feed on the yeast microbiota that metabolize decaying fruits and thus display attraction to volatiles arising from fermentation15,24. We therefore used apple cider vinegar (ACV), a broadly appetitive fermentation product, as a generic ‘host’ odour to compare how the chemical environment influences mating behaviours. Flies were fed and maintained as virgins in these assays to minimize their motivation to track towards the odour source for purely metabolic needs or in search of an oviposition site.

a, Schematic of large group assay comprising five males and five females in 190-mm arena with a 21.5-mm central food patch. b,c, Top, overlaid trajectories (grey) from representative D. erecta (D. ere) (b) and D. melanogaster (D. mel) (c) assays with agar (left) or ACV patch (right). Trajectory of one fly highlighted in black. Bottom, raster plots depicting the position of each fly relative to the patch over the duration of the assay, aligned by first patch entry (n = 7–10 assays). Patch occupancy is indicated in blue (agar) and orange (ACV). Greyscale indicates linear distance to patch, with lighter shades indicating closer proximity. d–f, Copulations and patch occupancy in assays from b,c. Copulation locations in the presence of ACV (orange) or agar patch (blue) (d). Mean patch occupancy per assay (e). Fraction of females copulated per assay (f). g, Schematic of high-density group assay comprising five males and five females in 38-mm arena with a 21.5-mm food patch. h,i, Courtship index (h) and latency to male courtship initiation (i) for D. erecta (n = 7–8 assays) and D. melanogaster (n = 6 assays). j, Phylogenetic relationships50,51 (left) and courtship indices (right) for D. orena (D. ore; n = 4–5 assays), D. yakuba (D. yak; n = 6–7 assays), D. sechellia (D. sec; n = 7 assays) and D. elegans (D. ele; n = 11 assays) males in small-arena assays. k–m, Social interactions in small-arena assays from h. Probability (p) of courtship (mean ± s.e.) in the first 10 min (left) or 1 min (centre, right) after courtship initiation (court. init.); centre shows expanded interval corresponding to dotted box at left (l). Mean interaction rate of D. erecta males towards any other fly over the duration of an assay (bold line; individual assays, thin lines) (m, top). Ethograms from representative agar (left, blue) and ACV (right, orange) assays showing interactions with other males (open circles), females (closed circles) and copulations (red circles and lines) (m, bottom). Throughout the figure, data pertaining to agar and ACV are in blue and orange, respectively. Dots in e and f are assay means; dots in h–j are individual males; horizontal bars in dot plots represent the mean. NS, not significant; *P ≤ 0.05; **P < 0.001; ***P < 0.0001. See Supplementary Table 1 for full statistics.

We found that in the context of the localized ACV patch, these two ecologically disparate species displayed distinct patterns of behaviour. D. melanogaster broadly explored the arena, giving rise to a dispersed spatial distribution where individuals interacted mostly in pairs and only intermittently in larger groups (Fig. 1c, Extended Data Fig. 1a–e and Supplementary Video 1). By contrast, D. erecta individuals rapidly approached the central ACV patch and remained there for extended bouts (Fig. 1b,e and Extended Data Fig. 1a,b), forming dynamic clusters of three or more interacting flies (Extended Data Fig. 1c–e). D. erecta did not congregate on a patch composed of agar alone (Fig. 1b,e, Extended Data Fig. 1b,f,g and Supplementary Video 1), indicating that food volatiles act as a potent aggregation cue in this species. Consistent with the notion that aggregation serves a social function in D. erecta, more than 90% of their copulations occurred on the ACV patch, in comparison to the spatially dispersed mating observed in D. melanogaster (Fig. 1d,f and Extended Data Fig. 1h). Comparable differences in aggregation and mating behaviour were also apparent when D. erecta and D. melanogaster were presented with a food patch made from the ripe pulp of D. erecta’s native host Pandanus candelabrum (Extended Data Fig. 1i–l), aligned with evidence that ACV shares several key volatiles with the bouquet of fermenting Pandanus fruit25,26,27. Notably, D. erecta refrained from mating entirely in the absence of ACV or Pandanus (Fig. 1f), highlighting the importance of the food patch as a site of reproductive opportunities in this species.

The ACV patch could facilitate mating in D. erecta by simply aggregating individuals, creating a dense social landscape where interactions between males and females are enhanced by proximity. Alternatively, ACV may directly elevate the sexual arousal of males or females on their arrival to the patch. To differentiate between these possibilities, we assessed the courtship dynamics of groups of five males and five females confined to a smaller chamber (diameter 38 mm, 4% area of the large arena; Fig. 1g), allowing us to decouple the effect of spatial proximity from the influence of the chemosensory environment. D. melanogaster males courted vigorously in this arena, independent of the presence of ACV (Fig. 1h and Supplementary Video 2). By contrast, D. erecta males courted only when ACV was present but rarely in its absence, despite the high density of flies (Fig. 1h,i and Supplementary Video 2). Indeed, D. erecta remained dispersed on an agar-only patch (Fig. 1k and Extended Data Fig. 2a), with males rarely approaching or pursuing individuals of either sex (Fig. 1m and Extended Data Fig. 2b,c). In the presence of ACV, however, the spatial distribution of D. erecta individuals was transformed, displaying a pronounced peak at 3 mm (Fig. 1k)—the interfly distance characteristic of courtship pursuit—along with a broad tail, reflecting the dynamic interactions of males as they indiscriminately advanced towards any individual who came into their field of view (FOV) (Fig. 1m and Extended Data Fig. 2d). The rare instances of D. erecta courtship on agar were transient, in contrast to the persistent pursuit observed in the presence of ACV (Fig. 1l,m). ACV thus seems to influence mating behaviours in D. erecta not simply by aggregating males and females but by restructuring their social dynamics.

Different strains of D. melanogaster vary markedly in their sensitivity to courtship cues28. Nevertheless, several strains, including a Cameroonian isolate collected within the overlapping geographic range of D. erecta, courted vigorously even in the absence of ACV (Extended Data Fig. 2e), indicating that the lack of reliance on this environmental signal is a broadly shared trait in this species. Although the limited availability of D. erecta strains precluded a comparable analysis of intraspecific variation, these results indicate that the food volatiles of ACV in D. melanogaster and D. erecta cannot be readily explained by variation within species and instead point to species-level differences in the sensory control of courtship. We therefore extended our analyses to related Drosophila species with distinct host ecologies. Unlike D. erecta, its sister species Drosophila orena, which specializes on Syzygium waterberries18, the closely related generalist Drosophila yakuba16 and the more distantly related specialist Drosophila sechellia, which breeds on Morinda citrifolia17, all vigorously courted conspecifics in both the presence and absence of ACV (Fig. 1j). By contrast, ACV suppressed courtship in D. elegans, a specialist that reproduces on Ipomoea blossoms19, potentially reflecting the limited chemical overlap between ACV and the volatile bouquet of its floral host29. Thus, although the influence of the chemosensory environment on reproductive behaviours varies across species, D. erecta males appear to have evolved a unique dependence on food volatiles to promote their courtship.

How does the chemosensory environment transform the structure of the D. erecta social landscape? Because interactions between individuals were more frequent on ACV, we reasoned that food odours may heighten the salience of visual objects. To explore this possibility, we presented individual males with a stationary fly-sized target—a high-contrast hemispherical bead, 3 mm in diameter (Fig. 2a)—and assessed whether ACV altered their interactions with it. D. melanogaster males were largely indifferent to this visual target, independent of the presence of ACV, spending most of their time circling the perimeter of the arena. D. erecta males, by contrast, remained in close proximity to the bead, an effect that was enhanced by ACV (Fig. 2b,c, Extended Data Fig. 3a–d and Supplementary Video 3). Optogenetic activation of most olfactory sensory neurons using the Orco promoter (Fig. 2d), which replicates the attractive valence of ACV in D. melanogaster30, was sufficient to promote attraction to the bead in D. erecta males on agar, confirming that olfactory input underlies this shift in visual salience (Fig. 2e,f, Extended Data Fig. 3e,f and Supplementary Video 4). Visual approach was not enhanced by the same optogenetic manipulation in D. melanogaster males, underscoring that in D. erecta, olfactory input exerts a species-specific influence on how males interact with their visual surroundings.

Colour bar indicates relative density. c, Left, trajectories of males in b during the first minute after a fly comes within 3 mm of the bead. Right, bead approaches per minute. d, Left, schematic of olfactory appendages innervated by Orco+ sensory neurons (green). Centre, their projections to the antennal lobes (green). Despite the strong attraction of D. erecta males to the bead on ACV, they frequently walked away before returning to it, generating a distinctive radial pattern as males alternated between approach and retreat (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Video 3), suggesting that the olfactory environment may also promote visual exploration. To examine this, we placed five D. erecta males in a large arena (diameter 190 mm) decorated with a lattice of 13 beads arranged in a regular square array (Fig. 2g; distance along edge 30 mm). In the presence of ACV, males spent most of their time near one of the targets but also frequently traversed between them (Extended Data Fig. 3h,i), often taking the shortest route (Fig. 2h–l and Supplementary Video 5). On agar, males restricted their exploration to a small fraction of the arena, remaining at their starting location or near the bead closest to it and rarely visiting any other visual targets (Fig. 2h–l, Extended Data Fig. 3h,i and Supplementary Video 5). Comparing the trajectories of solitary males showed that they display a similar shift in their behaviour in the presence of ACV (Extended Data Fig. 3j), indicating that visual sampling is driven by the chemical, not social, context. Without the bead lattice, males on ACV showed no spatial bias and remained broadly distributed across the arena (Extended Data Fig. 3h). By contrast, the visual exploration of D. melanogaster males was unaffected by the chemosensory environment (Extended Data Fig. 3k–o). Olfactory cues thus selectively promote exploration in D. erecta males.

Beads, although attractive visual targets to males, rarely evoked courtship displays such as the wing extensions associated with song production, indicating they are not perceived as potential mates (Extended Data Fig. 3p). Indeed, replacing a single bead in the array with a decapitated female shifted the search dynamics of males: on encountering the female, males often terminated their exploration and maintained her at close range (Fig. 2m,n and Extended Data Fig. 3q,r). Males occasionally resumed exploration of nearby beads after encountering the female but now often sang as they approached (Fig. 2o), indicating that the distinct cuticular pheromones carried by D. erecta females altered the males’ interpretation of visual targets, triggering a shift from exploration to courtship. Males on agar failed to locate the female in the bead lattice (Fig. 2p), suggesting that their limited exploration in the absence of food volatiles hinders their ability to detect or pursue prospective female mates. Thus, ACV promotes locomotion in D. erecta males to drive more frequent sampling of visual objects in their environment, supporting a form of ‘social foraging’ in which they search for reproductive opportunities rather than food resources.

In D. melanogaster, courtship is triggered by recognition of an appropriate conspecific female, a behavioural switch mediated by a network of male-specific P1 neurons that integrate multisensory signals—including direct excitatory input from pheromone pathways—to gate entry into a persistent arousal state31,32,33,34. D. erecta females, like their D. melanogaster counterparts, produce sex- and species-specific cuticular hydrocarbons35 that robustly excite the P1 neurons of conspecific males36, indicating that they similarly serve as chemical determinants of mate recognition. Food volatiles could therefore facilitate D. erecta courtship simply by encouraging males to approach females and sample their pheromonal cues. Yet even in the rare instances when D. erecta males initiated courtship on agar, their pursuit was fleeting (Fig. 1l,m), pointing to the possibility that food volatiles are required not only to promote encounters with females but also to sustain male sexual arousal in this species.

Consistent with this, although optogenetic activation of P1 neurons in D. melanogaster is sufficient to evoke persistent courtship37,38, in D. erecta it triggered only transient courtship bouts towards an immobilized female in the absence of ACV, with males rapidly resuming indifference after the optogenetic stimulus (Fig. 3a,b). By contrast, in the presence of ACV, P1 neuron activation drove sustained courtship in D. erecta males, suggesting that although P1 neurons promote entry into a state of sexual arousal, olfactory cues are required for its perpetuation. This olfactory dependence extended to pursuit of a moving visual target. In the absence of ACV, P1 neuron activation evoked only brief bouts of courtship towards a fly-sized 3-mm projected dot rotating on the floor of the assay chamber, whereas in the presence of ACV, males pursued and sang to the target spontaneously, even without P1 activation (Fig. 3c–f and Supplementary Videos 6 and 7).

To determine whether continuous olfactory input is required to sustain a male’s arousal, we leveraged the fact that tethered males will spontaneously court a fly-sized visual target projected onto a panorama, faithfully tracking its motion while singing to it38 (Fig. 4a). D. erecta males were largely indifferent to this visual target alone but initiated robust pursuit upon presentation of ACV (Fig. 4b,c,e,f, Extended Data Fig. 4 and Supplementary Video 8). Notably, courtship tracking was transient, with males rapidly terminating their pursuit at the offset of the odour stimulus, reinforcing that ACV is required for the perpetuation of arousal (Fig. 4e,f and Extended Data Fig. 4b–d). D. melanogaster males, by contrast, commenced courtship pursuit at the onset of the visual stimulus and persistently tracked it for the duration of the assay (Fig. 4c,e,f), consistent with evidence that visual cues are sufficient to arouse males of this species, even in the absence of further sensory feedback33,38 (Extended Data Fig. 5).

In D. melanogaster, P1 neurons dynamically modulate the gain of LC10a visual projection neurons via a multisynaptic pathway38,39 (Fig. 4d), forming a concise visuomotor circuit that mediates a male’s faithful courtship pursuit when he is sexually aroused. To assess whether this gain control mechanism is conserved, we generated selective genetic drivers that allowed us to record activity from P1 or LC10a neurons in D. erecta males during courtship pursuit. Despite the divergent sensory dependencies of courtship across species, the activity of P1 neurons was correlated with bouts of pursuit in both D. erecta and D. melanogaster (Fig. 4e and Extended Data Fig. 6). Likewise, LC10a visual responses were amplified during courtship in both species, with robust activation each time the target swept in the progressive direction across the male’s ipsilateral visual field during epochs of active pursuit (Fig. 4f and Extended Data Fig. 7a–c). These observations point to a conserved circuit organization in which the gain of LC10a visual responses is dynamically modulated by a male’s sexual arousal to orchestrate mate pursuit in both species. However, whereas visual cues alone are sufficient to vigorously arouse D. melanogaster males, D. erecta males additionally require continuous olfactory input, which appears to act as a stringent species-specific gate to sustain courtship in this species.

Notably, neither LC10a neurons nor the subset of P1 neurons labelled by our genetic driver were activated by ACV (Fig. 4g), indicating that food volatiles do not sustain arousal through direct olfactory input to these conserved circuit components. Moreover, ACV did not alter P1 responses to female pheromones in either D. erecta or D. melanogaster males (Fig. 4h), reinforcing that food odours do not simply tune the excitability of this integrative node to control a male’s arousal. Rather, we found that ACV activates an array of distributed neurons labelled by the sexually dimorphic Fruitless (Fru) and Doublesex (Dsx) transcription factors (Extended Data Figs. 7d–j and 8). These include subsets of neurons innervating the anterior optic tubercle (AOTu), to which LC10a neurons send their axonal projections, and the lateral protocerebral complex (LPC), which is richly innervated by P1 neurons, consistent with olfactory pathways responsive to environmental food odours converging with sexually dimorphic courtship circuits.

Within the LPC, conspecific female pheromones and ACV activated spatially segregated populations of dsx-expressing neurons, suggesting that sexual and environmental chemosensory signals impinge on these central courtship circuits through parallel pathways (Extended Data Fig. 8). This functional organization aligns with connectomic analyses in D. melanogaster, which show that distinct sensory pathways controlling male courtship act through different subsets of P1 neurons and their downstream targets34. Similar spatially segregated responses to female pheromones and ACV were also apparent in the LPC of D. melanogaster and D. yakuba males (Extended Data Fig. 8), species that court conspecifics regardless of the presence of food volatiles (Fig. 1h,j). The conservation of ACV-responsive populations across species may therefore provide a neural substrate for the latent potential of food odours to promote courtship when other sensory cues are experimentally impoverished, such as in the presence of inanimate visual targets (Extended Data Fig. 5). Despite this conservation, among the species we examined, D. erecta males uniquely depend on ACV to sustain courtship of conspecific females, even when P1 neurons are activated to trigger a state of sexual arousal (Fig. 3b,d). Thus, environmental olfactory signals appear to be differentially weighted across species, serving as a stringent gate for persistent sexual arousal in D. erecta, potentially through sexually dimorphic regulatory nodes that interact with, but remain distinct from, the circuitry mediating mate recognition. In support of this possibility, D. erecta males still discriminate between potential mates even when highly aroused on a food patch, avoiding courtship of unsuitable heterospecific females on the basis of the detection of their inhibitory pheromones (Extended Data Fig. 9a).

How do environmental food volatiles and visual cues coordinately shape male behaviour in naturalistic contexts, where many flies aggregate on a food patch? By driving D. erecta males to sample and pursue visual targets (Fig. 2), ACV results in an increase in fly locomotion that scales with the size of the group (Extended Data Fig. 9b–d). In the context of larger aggregates of flies, this odour-dependent shift in locomotion dramatically altered each male’s visual experience (Fig. 5a–e), expanding the fraction of his visual field occupied by other flies (Fig. 5d) and increasing the visual motion sweeping across his retina (Fig. 5a–c,e). Notably, males and females continued to generate motion cues even when copulating, as D. erecta females reliably began to spin while mounted (Supplementary Video 2). The motion generated by interacting individuals on a food patch thus transforms the visual backdrop, suggesting that it may convey broader information about social context to further control male arousal. Indeed, even on agar, males displayed correlated bursts of locomotor activity and courtship (Fig. 5f,g, Extended Data Fig. 9e,f and Supplementary Video 9), consistent with the motion cues emanating from nearby flies transiently elevating male arousal. These observations point to a feedback loop in which ACV both promotes courtship and reshapes the sensory landscape in which courtship unfolds.
