#1160. Why are we conscious? Nature investigates the theories

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Amanda Heidt is a freelance journalist in southeast Utah.

Imaging can be used to measure the degree of variation and complexity across brain regions that correspond to conscious states.Credit: AJ Photo/Hop Americain/SPL

At first glance, human consciousness seems like the one thing we should never have to doubt. We know we are conscious because we experience the world in vivid detail: the small luxury of a piece of chocolate; a song imbued with sadness; or a childhood memory that takes us back to another place and time.

But for such a fundamental aspect of reality, what underlies consciousness — the experience of being aware of one’s own existence — has proved deceptively hard to pin down. Researchers and philosophers have spent centuries debating how and why physical processes in the brain result in the subjective, first-person experiences we all seem to have. This issue, known as the ‘hard problem’ of consciousness, continues to drive research today.

Scientists are still far from explaining how brain activity begets an entire inner world, but the field is making progress. The advances that researchers have made include the ability to reliably measure brain activity and connectedness and probe for signs of hidden awareness.

The emerging picture — based on insights from not just neuroscience, but also far-flung disciplines such as plant science, artificial intelligence and astrobiology — is not of consciousness as a single light that can be switched on, but as a coordinated condition that is potentially more widespread than previously thought. The rapid rise of AI, for example, has fuelled discussions over whether only humans can be conscious — and of whether a brain is even required for consciousness.

“People are often troubled by the fact that our understanding remains somewhat vague,” says Matthias Michel, a philosopher of cognitive science at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge. “However, it’s very important to note that definitions in the history of science come at the end of the scientific process, not at the beginning. I’d argue we’re now in the thick of it, which is an exciting place to be.”

There is no direct test for evaluating human consciousness, but researchers have made advances in establishing what are known as neural correlates of consciousness (NCCs). These criteria, which can be a single metric or a combination of events, identify the minimum neuronal mechanism required to kickstart a conscious experience. Specific neurons might need to fire, for example, and particular brain activity patterns could signify an internal experience. Below these thresholds, a person might move through life not fully conscious of their behaviour — zoning out while driving, for instance, only to snap back to attention moments later.

Some NCCs have been determined by studying people in states we don’t typically associate with consciousness, such as those who are asleep, anaesthetized or in a coma. According to Melanie Boly, a neurologist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, this type of research is crucial to help separate true NCCs from activities that merely signify being awake and responsive to our surroundings.

“That’s been a big breakthrough, isolating the true features of consciousness, rather than simply measuring something that is associated with or a consequence of the conscious experience,” Boly says.

Is social media changing children’s brains? Here’s what the science says

Is social media changing children’s brains? Here’s what the science says

Through that work, scientists know that about one-quarter of individuals who present as medically unconscious are, in fact, experiencing a type of covert consciousness in which they continue to perceive the world around them. In a landmark 2024 study, a subset of 241 people who had been left seemingly unresponsive by brain injuries were asked to imagine themselves engaging in activities such as playing tennis or opening and closing their hand. Dozens of patients’ brains became active on imaging scans during these challenges — calling into question whether consciousness persists in otherwise-inert states1.

In recognition of this finding, researchers have moved away from thinking of consciousness as a binary experience towards an understanding that consciousness is a dynamic process that exists on a continuum. From these principles, it has been possible to develop metrics that test the underlying scientific assumptions about consciousness. One of the most promising of these is called the perturbational complexity index (PCI)2.

PCI evaluates a person’s level of consciousness by assessing how their brain responds to a brief magnetic pulse, as measured by electroencephalography (EEG), which traces the brain’s electrical activity using electrodes. In a conscious brain, the neural response usually spreads while remaining complex and distinct from one brain region to another — features referred to as integration and differentiation, respectively. During sleep or under anaesthesia, the response becomes simpler and more repetitive.

“PCI is considered to be a very accurate correlate of consciousness that can be useful in many research settings,” says Johan Frederik Storm, a neurophysiologist at the University of Oslo. Widespread clinical adoption has unfortunately been hampered by the fact that it’s a laborious metric to gather, he adds, “but even still, it is gaining traction”.

This growing understanding has led to the development of hypotheses that move beyond simply measuring aspects of consciousness towards a more foundational understanding of what it is. At present, there are more than 450 such theories, many of which share overlapping features even as they distinguish themselves by scale or focus. The two most popular are the global neuronal workspace theory (GNWT) and the integrated information theory (IIT).

The GNWT posits that most brain activity is restricted to specialized areas — visual regions process shapes and colours, for example, and language areas process words. Consciousness emerges when information becomes important enough to be broadcast across regions. A face whose representation remains inside the visual system might trigger a simple, unconscious reaction, but a face that triggers regions across the brain, collectively known as the global workspace, can be used by many systems to build a conscious experience.

The IIT tries to answer a different question: what is experience like? When we view the world or recall a memory, we experience a cohesive scene, not separate elements of colour, sound and touch. The IIT argues that consciousness depends on how strongly the parts of a system affect one another while still remaining distinct — there must be both integration and differentiation to give rise to diverse states and experiences. A conscious system must be more than a collection of independent parts, and it must form a whole that has a state that cannot be fully explained by looking at each part separately.

A major issue with proving such hypotheses is that researchers have often tested them in ways that lack true neutrality and rigour. A 2022 analysis of hundreds of experiments found that research into consciousness has often been done in ways that pre-emptively bias the results in support of a particular theory3. This has made it a challenge to directly compare studies of consciousness, according to Christof Koch, a consciousness researcher at the Allen Institute for Brain Science in Seattle, Washington, who has studied the topic for decades.

“People become very attached to their theories, and that confirmation bias can sometimes get in the way of an honest, collaborative effort,” he says.

Lucia Melloni, a cognitive neuroscientist at the Ruhr University Bochum in Germany, recently led a first-of-its-kind effort to force a direct comparison of the two schools of thought. She brought together proponents of both theories, as well as neutral participants, and asked them to agree in advance to a set of experiments and predictions. The group probed foundational assumptions of both theories4 using three measurement techniques — EEG; functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which tracks brain activity by detecting tiny changes in blood flow; and magnetoencephalography (MEG), which measures magnetic fields produced by the brain’s electrical currents.

Plants lack brains, but are capable of decision-making and problem-solving.Credit: Jason Milligan/Courtesy of Understory

One of the main differences between the two ideas is which part of the brain is considered most essential to the act of being. The GNWT predicts a sudden ‘ignition’ of widespread brain activity when a stimulus prompts a conscious experience, and so the prefrontal cortex is expected to play an important part because it uses information to form complex behaviours. ITT focuses instead on a ‘hot zone’ located towards the back of the brain that includes parts of the systems responsible for vision, hearing and touch, because it follows that this is where the relevant stimuli converge to generate a full experience.

The team found conscious information represented in both regions. However, the results also challenged important predictions of both theories. The long-lasting activity predicted by the IIT to occur in the back of the cortex was not clearly represented, and the ignition expected by the GNWT was limited. As such, the study did not settle the debate, instead suggesting that both theories might offer parts of an answer.

Melloni doesn’t see this as a failure, and considers such results the most exciting outcome. “I’m happy with what we found because neither theory was left untouched,” she says. “Having your predictions confirmed doesn’t leave you anywhere to grow, whereas having your thinking challenged makes you do better science.”

One way that scientists are attempting to expand their thinking is through interdisciplinary collaborations, drawing evidence from fields as distant as plant and non-human animal biology, robotics and even the search for extraterrestrial life to flesh out the conditions under which consciousness can arise. It’s not certain, for instance, that brains — or even neurons — are required. Astrobiologists have long been searching for sentient life, yet given the expanse of the known Universe, they cannot reasonably assume it will look anything like us.

#1158. What's wrong with Kai Havertz and can he fix it in time for Liverpool vs. Arsenal showdown

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

If last season's visit to Anfield taught Arsenal anything, it was the need for a killer in the final third to break the game open. Fail to do so and they are vulnerable to the sort of magic that bamboozled them in August of last year, even if the man who scored that brilliant free-kick winner, Dominik Szoboszlai, is a doubt for Liverpool on Sunday.

And if this game is indeed one that will be decided by what Mikel Arteta terms the "moments players," then it could scarcely have come at a worse time for the Arsenal manager. Bukayo Saka -- the Gunners' top shot taker, goal scorer and expected goals compiler -- has more than a month left on the sidelines with the thigh injury he suffered in Munich. Noni Madueke could miss the trip with an ankle injury. Christos Tzolis has returned to training but has not played for his new club in more than a month. Max Dowman, the precocious youngster whom Arteta has already entrusted with turning the tide on Merseyside, will serve the first of a three-game ban for his controversial red card.

It speaks to the depth at Arteta's disposal that, even if none of the aforementioned quartet play, there will still be game changers in the side. Even so, this does feel like an occasion where a first-choice center forward in top form would be handy. Kai Havertz is not that. Twelve games in and this has been perhaps the weirdest season of all since this esoteric forward landed on English soil in 2020. At his best, he has blown his former club Chelsea away. His worst, meanwhile, includes a wasteful performance in the EFL Cup defeat at Fleetwood and a baffling new tendency to slip offside.

The obvious answer when a player slides from peak to trough in a matter of weeks is to consult his injury record. Havertz did return from the last international break early after straining a muscle and went straight back into the side, playing an hour against Leeds and featuring in every other game since. In those six games he has no goals and one assist. In most of the minutes he has played, he has struggled to link the Arsenal attack together the way he usually does, let alone to threaten the opposition goal. That is not, however, a hangover from his injury travails.

"There's nothing to do with that," said Arteta. "It's true that in terms of the numbers, we have dropped those numbers but he certainly had the chances as well to play."

That was the case against Fleetwood, seven shots for the German adding up to 0.72 expected goals. That sounds perfectly adequate on first pass, and there are certainly others in the Arsenal side who ought to have asked more of a League Two defense. And yet when chasing a game for 70 minutes, is it fair to ask for more than three-quarters of an xG from the senior attacker of the English champions, a man who has scored in two Champions League finals?

Wanting a bit more has been a familiar experience for both Chelsea and Arsenal during his time with them. For the Gunners, it has been over two and a half years since they discovered just how good Havertz could be for them. The shift to center forward in a 3-1 win over Sunday's opponents, Liverpool, was the start of a brilliant year leading the line. Across 37 Premier League games, the Germany international delivered 18 goals and nine assists, not Erling Haaland numbers but exceptional output for the center forward in Arteta's everyone-eats offense.

Even since that brilliant run, there have been flashes. For an hour in May's Champions League final, Havertz was as threatening an attacker as anyone in PSG colors. A few weeks earlier he had been excellent in defeat to Manchester City, not the first time he had bossed Arsenal's title rival. If Chelsea have the misfortune of running into their former star, they're probably going to get him in the mood to do some damage. Of all the attackers available to Arteta this week, Havertz is the nearest he has to a big-game hunter. Indeed, if you want to make the case against Arsenal "just signing a striker" in January (you shouldn't), a key component of your argument ought to be how few players suit this manager as well as a fully fit Havertz. It is just that, well, a fully fit Havertz has been an elusive creature. And yet if Arteta will not use injuries as justification for the current wobble, perhaps we shouldn't. And wobble this is. Through eight league games, Havertz is averaging fewer shots, goals and non-penalty xG than in any other season in his Arsenal career on a per-90 basis. The same is true when you adjust for the fact that the 27-year-old is touching the ball a bit less on average this season than last. There is one notable stat where Havertz's numbers have skyrocketed, though, and that is in offsides. In every Premier League season before this one, he was caught out behind the opposition defense on less than one occasion per 90 minutes. In most of them, he averaged around one offside per two full games played. This year, however, no one in the league matches Havertz's 10 offsides already, and the gap is not particularly close. Joint-second on seven are his teammate Bukayo Saka and Dominic Calvert-Lewin of Leeds.

Now, the sample size of minutes is still small and open to distortion. It might be that one explanation for Havertz's skyrocketing offsides is that he has played Aston Villa and their occasionally effective, invariably cavalier high line. Equally, not all of those 10 offsides are about what the defense did well or about a run that came at just the wrong moment from the center forward. Watch Havertz move a good moment too soon to collect a pass off his friend and captain Martin Odegaard before bending well wide from a promising shooting position against Villa, and you see what looks like a forward who is simply off color, nothing more and nothing less, really. Sometimes the easiest explanation is the correct one. Havertz is just a bit out of sync with both his game and that of his teammates, as his manager acknowledged on Friday.

"That kind of form and that kind of efficiency with the front players, it's very common," said Arteta. "Full trust on him and what he's doing."

The natural response, then, for Arteta would be to pick the next cab off the rank, as he did in the win over Everton where Viktor Gyokeres started. That was the Swede's best game of the season, but he still did not register a shot. Gyokeres scored against Fleetwood but took only two other shots. Per 90, he averages 0.92 shots, 16th on Arsenal, with both left backs ahead of him. The evidence of his past entanglements with elite opposition suggests that Gyokeres is not the player to turn to at Anfield.

Instead, it will be Havertz, in need of something of a jump-start to his season. While he retains the "full trust" of a manager who has never faltered in his support, there might be time enough to sniff out his best form.

#1156. Manchester United stick with Michael Carrick ahead of Chelsea matchup as dressing-room discord fuels crisis

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

To the surprise of many, Michael Carrick will continue to be in the dugout for Manchester United as they face Chelsea on Saturday. During their eight-game winless run in all competitions, United have allowed 15 goals while scoring six, and off the pitch, everything is unraveling, with players and fans alike questioning the direction of the club. United have been in this position before, and it has usually led to a change of manager and a rebuild of the club from the ground up. But what's different is that during this rut, players are publicly speaking out. While things will sometimes leak via undisclosed sources, players saying the quiet part out loud about what's going on with the club is not a good look. Defender Lisandro Martinez spoke about the need for the club to have higher standards and claimed that it's lacking ambition after a poor loss to Atletico Madrid in Champions League play, but it went from bad to worse as captain Bruno Fernandes spoke out after a humbling loss to Como, questioning the team's tactics.

Date: Saturday, Oct. 31 | Time: 8:30 a.m. ETLocation: Stamford Bridge  -- LondonTV: USA NetworkOdds: Chelsea -105; Draw +270; Manchester United +270

That led to Fernandes being benched and United failing yet again to pick up a victory. While the public view is that Fernandes will retain his captaincy, the episode has to strip away at least some of Carrick's authority within the club. "There is no decision to be made on [the captaincy]," Carrick said. "It will be Bruno. Listen, we're clear with the situation of the team and as a football club at the moment. He's an important player for this group. He has been and he will be." Ahead of a match where both teams are struggling, the slightest lack of balance could lead to yet another United loss. With no clear sign that authority lies with the manager rather than the captain, especially after Carrick held meetings about the future of his job, this could get worse before it gets better. What do you do if United concede an early goal and the match goes off the rails? On the evidence we've seen, it's tough to say Carrick will be able to get the club out of that spiral, and if he can't, there's no reason why he should be the manager. On paper, while too much money was invested in the midfield instead of defense, this isn't a bad squad, but United find themselves in the relegation race only one season after qualifying for Champions League play. Even their numbers scream midtable, not doomed to relegation.

That's where the mentality of the squad comes in. It's been a persistent issue since Sir Alex Ferguson left, and it's not an issue that seems to be going away anytime soon. At times, it will lie dormant for a season during which you think United are righting the ship, only to come back at the worst time possible. Carrick is only a symptom of a larger issue at Manchester United, and the club has gone through eight permanent managers since Ferguson without sustained success. It's not for lack of spending, and even though there are questions around who is recruited, for the most part, the squads have been fine. They just can never perform to the sum of their parts.

Since Jim Ratcliffe took over, the club has been more focused on profits off the pitch than actual success on it, and that's catching up with United. Turning that around is going to be quite a challenge. Fan protests have been seen, but they aren't igniting real change, and we may be in a situation where United need a sustained spell in the bottom half of the table to lead to anything different. In short, this is already dire, and every day with Carrick at the helm delays the start of that turnaround, even if that isn't his fault. United have become a club without a direction, and that's something Chelsea can take advantage of as the Xabi Alonso era at Stamford Bridge has signs of success but needs a result to get back on the right track.

#1154. MLS reveals 2027 sprint season schedule ahead of shift to European calendar

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

While the MLS regular season has yet to come to a close, the details of the sprint season have now been released. The sprint season is a critical bridge to the league moving to a European calendar, as the 2027 season will take place under a condensed schedule in order to prepare for that. Each team will play 14 regular season matches, with one home and one away. The regular season will run from February 19, with Inter Miami and FC Cincinnati kicking things off, until Decision Day on May 8t, when there's a Hudson River Derby between New York City FC and New York Red Bulls to close out the season. With NYCFC set to open a new stadium in Queens, this should also be the final MLS game played at Yankee Stadium, which NYCFC have called home since joining the league in 2015. Truly the end of an era that went on for far too long.

Ahead of the shift, MLS wants to ensure that each week has a marquee matchup to highlight the best of what the league has to offer. There will also be another season of the Walmart Saturday Showdown and of Sunday Night Soccer, so that the biggest games of the week get their due credit. With stars from abroad such as Antoine Griezmann, Lionel Messi, Thomas Muller, and Evander pitting against young stars such as Cavan Sullivan, Julian Hall, Adri Mehmeti, and Peyton Miller, there's plenty to showcase as MLS prepares for a new era.

It’s an all-out sprint. 👀The 2027 MLS Sprint Season Schedule is here. ⬇️✏️: https://t.co/5qDlJnxjeW pic.twitter.com/71brwLBgcV

The top eight teams in each conference will qualify for the playoffs, with each round being played in a single-elimination format. That schedule is yet to be announced, but it will see a shift from the current format, where the eighth- and ninth-placed teams play a single-elimination wild card match prior to the first round being a best-of-three series. That playoff format has seen criticism due to being too long, so the sprint season does offer an opportunity to take a look at other formats ahead of a return to a standard schedule in the fall. Still, using playoffs will ensure that all five Concacaf Champions Cup spots are accounted for before the teams also return to full participation in the Lamar Hunt U.S. Open Cup

This split will help get MLS onto the same transfer market as the rest of the world. MLS doing their primary transfer window in the winter has long been an issue due to teams not being able to send players to America. It also could mean that MLS sides won't be pressured to sell their best players midseason, either with the summer transfer window being an enticing time for teams to wade in and get new players during their own preseason. The change will bring geographic challenges such as dealing with harsh winters, but those are no different from the thunderstorm and extreme heat risks that the league already faces during the summer months in such varied climates. With the shift also including teams stopping play for international breaks, it will also end the need to play without your best players available, which increases the quality in the league.

Following the conclusion of this sprint season, the 2027-28 MLS Season will kick off in July of 2027. It will then conclude with the MLS Cup playoffs, which will run until May of 2028, similarly to when most European leagues wrap up.

#1152. World Cup qualifier suspended after sinkhole opens up on pitch

Play was brought to a standstill during Austriaâs 2026 World Cup qualifier against Cyprus after a sinkhole suddenly appeared on the pitch late in the second half.

The bizarre incident occurred around the 75th minute, when Danish referee Jakob Kehlet halted the match after noticing the gaping hole near Austria keeper Alexander Schlagerâs box at the Raiffeisen Arena, in Linz.

The opening was wide enough to swallow an entire football, prompting ground staff to rush on with buckets of sand in a frantic attempt to patch it up.

After more than seven minutes of repairs, Kehlet finally gave the green light to resume, with Austria eventually sealing a 1-0 win thanks to Marcel Sabitzerâs second-half penalty â scored before the ground gave way.

A section of the pitch has literally collapsed in the game between Austria & Cyprus. The ground staff are running up and down with buckets of soil trying to sort the situation. Canât remember seeing anything like it! pic.twitter.com/OECrF5jiGk

The win means Austria are now second in Group H qualifying, having won all three of their games so far, behind also unbeaten Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Remarkably, this isnât the first time Austrian football has flirted with the earth caving in. Back in 2022, a Nations League clash against Denmark, which Austria lost 2-1, at the Ernst Happel Stadium was also interrupted by a huge sinkhole opening up on the pitch.

At least this time Austria still managed to dig out the three points â though maybe someone in should be calling a geologist before the next fixture.

#1151. Harry Kane ends England’s 25-year wait for Ballon d’Or winner

“Wow, wow, wow,” Harry Kane said as he took to the stage at the London Palladium after winning the 2026 Ballon d’Or. Wow indeed. “I am speechless,” Kane added before launching into a heartfelt speech, the wobble in his voice showing just how much this meant to him.

In truth it would have been a travesty had the 33-year-old England captain – and Bayern Munich striker – not won with his family, friends and coaches all watching from the stalls at this famous old theatre. “All those years of sacrifice,” he said of his parents, Pat and Kim, his voice faltering more than ever at that moment. It was from the heart. And faltering again as he spoke about his wife and “best friend” Katie Goodland. “This is a trophy we all celebrate,” he said, talking to his children back in Bavaria. “I bring a few others [trophies] home but this one is a special one.”

Kane’s speech was as outstanding as his football. “Lastly for me it is the journey,” he said. “Learn through resilience, determination and self-belief. My journey was not easy and I had to fight my way to be the very best right now. I hope that can give you inspiration.”

So much for the “one-season wonder”. So much for the doubters who poured scorn on him. So much for those who believed he would never make it after loan spells at Leyton Orient, Millwall, Norwich City and Leicester City. With varying degrees of success.

Kate Scott, the presenter, perfectly detected the emotion and said: “You held it together. You got through it.” It showed how much it meant to Kane, who simply and quietly replied: “Yes”.

What a winner. What a player. What a role model. The award given in the city where he has scored most of his goals. But he would not have been in the running for this accolade had he not been brave enough to quit Tottenham Hotspur after 19 years and move to Germany.

Kane was the favourite. But, despite its prestige, the Ballon d’Or process is an odd one. One journalist from each of the top-100-ranked Fifa countries is given a vote, with the organisers, France Football, laying out the criteria: individual performance, collective performance and fair play. In that order. They often go for the biggest name. Not the best.

Kane’s numbers are incredible. They speak for themselves. Those numbers show he deserved to win the prize: 65 games for club and country and 73 goals. Plus eight assists (for the judging period – August 3, 2025 to July 19, 2026). That is 61 goals for Bayern and 12 for England. That is a goal less than every 72 minutes. That is beyond elite. That is world class and legendary.

Bayern Munich and England's Ballon d'Or winner doing what he does best 🎯 https://t.co/yWNburqkpg

For his club, that is 19 goals more than any other player in the top five European leagues. And the most since Cristiano Ronaldo scored 61 for Real Madrid in 2014-15. Kane won last season’s Golden Shoe by nine goals from Erling Haaland. He reached his century of Bundesliga goals last month in just 98 games, destroying Dieter Müller’s record set 49 years ago – he took 129 matches.

Kane became one of only two players in history (the other is Ronaldo) to score 20-plus goals across World Cups and European Championships and was the only one to score in two major club cup finals, including a hat-trick. Neither Kylian Mbappé nor Lamine Yamal, his closest rivals, scored in any finals.

Both gave interviews declaring why they should win the Ballon d’Or. Kane? “I don’t like talking about myself,” he said. “The 73 goals speak for themselves.” They do.

Those are the facts, but there is also the football and, yes, the conduct. Kane has scored some superb goals during that period, not least for England. Take his two goals against the Democratic Republic of Congo at the World Cup that saved his team and Thomas Tuchel from an embarrassing early exit.

The Prince of Wales, who has been FA president since 2006, congratulated Kane on “a fantastic achievement”.

“A brilliant captain, a remarkable player and someone who has given football fans across the world so many unforgettable moments,” Prince William wrote on Instagram.

Kane, the first English player since Michael Owen in 2001 to win the award, is also the ultimate team player – so fulfilling that “collective performance” criteria – and a captain who leads by example on and off the pitch. Fair play? He was last booked in January and was cautioned just three times in 68 games and not at all in any of his 13 appearances this season.

And he works hard, so very hard. Kane was in the top 10 for total distance covered at the World Cup, despite playing a game fewer than most of the others on the list. And he is often seen winning as many defensive headers in his own penalty area as attacking ones in the opposition’s.

That work extends to off the pitch, to try to maximise his ability, to do everything to be the best version of himself and to be the best. Which he has now been recognised as. And it stems from his winning mentality. Some scoffed when Kane walked into England’s press conference before the 2018 World Cup and said he could be top-scorer – but he proved them wrong.

They probably also scoffed at the notion that he would one day be declared the best player in the world and win the Ballon d’Or. But he has done all that. It confirms England’s all-time cap holder (for now jointly with Peter Shilton) and goalscorer as one of the greats. And we are privileged to witness that greatness. Wow, what a night.

By Christian FalkGermany do not have a single player among the 30 in the running to win the Ballon d’Or in London on Monday night – but Bayern Munich do have England captain Harry Kane.

For the 35-time German champions, the award is perhaps even more important than it is for the peerless striker himself. The Bayern hierarchy are planning to travel to the Palladium Theatre en masse to support Kane.

Kane is not only Bayern’s top striker, he is their international figurehead and, internally, their poster-boy professional. Club patron and honorary president Uli Hoeness described the England captain as the best signing in the club’s history. Hoeness even went so far as to say he loves Kane, and he is not alone in this.

There's only one Harry Kane. https://t.co/NfZEFmjaUN

Hoeness is one of many in the club’s leadership who have been endlessly promoting Kane to help the 33-year-old fulfil his lifelong dream of winning the trophy. Bayern officials have been campaigning on his behalf for weeks.

First up was manager Vincent Kompany, who remains in hospital for tests after collapsing at Bayern’s training ground on Friday. Kompany said: “If he can now crown his career or his season with the Ballon d’Or, that would be fitting given the way he plays for the team.”

The plaudits kept coming. Whether it was sporting director Max Eberl (“He has more than earned the Ballon d’Or. Anyone who loves football loves characters like Harry Kane”), chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen (“One thing is clear – anyone talking about this year’s greatest individual honours cannot overlook Harry Kane”) or president Herbert Hainer (“Harry Kane embodies the idea that sporting greatness is incomplete without greatness of character. He would be a worthy World Footballer of the Year”), everyone at the club is fighting for Kane.

The official Ballon d’Or website has announced Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal as winners of the main prize in an embarrassing blunder for the organisation.

Three separate articles were published before quickly being taken down.

The headline on Kane’s article read: ‘Harry Kane wins 2026 Ballon d’Or: Here are his best and most meaningful strikes from a 61-goal season’.

The 70th Ballon d’Or ceremony takes place at the London Palladium as England and Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane aims to become the first Englishman in more than 20 years to win the award. Michael Owen was the last Englishman to win the award back in 2001.

The choice of London as the host city pays tribute to the award’s inaugural winner, England’s Stanley Matthews, who won it in 1956. This also marks the first time the ceremony will be organised outside France. Kane, who scored over 70 goals for club and country in the relevant year, is among the favourites for this year’s award alongside the likes of Barcelona and Spain’s Lamine Yamal and Real Madrid and France’s Kylian Mbappe.

Kane won the Bundesliga with Bayern Munich whereas Yamal won both La Liga and the World Cup. Yamal won the Kopa Trophy at last year’s ceremony as the best men’s young player.

Last year’s winners were Spain and Barcelona midfielder Aitana Bonmati and France and Barcelona forward Ousmane Dembele. Dembele is aiming to become just the 11th man to win the top prize at least twice, although it would appear to be very unlikely that the Frenchman will be winning the award this evening.

Selected international journalists cast their votes based on the performances of players throughout the season. The panel consists of one representative per country from the top 100 nations in the Fifa men’s world ranking and the top 50 in the women’s world ranking. Each voter ranks their top 10 candidates, with points distributed on a descending scale. They vote based on three factors: individual performance, team achievements, and class combined with fair play.

In total, 13 trophies will be presented across the men’s and women’s game, including the two man Ballon d’Or awards, the best young players and best teams. The awards take into account achievements from August 3, 2025, to July 19, 2026 (August 16 for the women).

#1146. Manchester United's players, not Michael Carrick, should shoulder the blame after embarrassing loss to Chelsea

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

LONDON -- Manchester United players have been at great pains in recent weeks to point out how they have been failed by the powers that be, by those with supposedly more influence than the 11 lads on the field. On occasion, you could argue they had the measure of the situation. There's just one little note for Lisandro Martinez, Bruno Fernandes and anyone else who counts themselves among the Old Trafford mutineers.

If you're going to start demanding greater professional standards from your employers, you would be well advised to hold yourself to the same level. It would be a real problem if, for instance, you earned yourself two yellow cards in the space of 210 seconds, handing your opponents the penalty from which they win the game. Sympathy will be in quite short supply for those who complain about the head coach's tactics or the sporting director's recruitment but then, when the circumstances are right, fail to exploit prime opportunities.

Lisandro Martinez was right when he intimated a fortnight ago that Jason Wilcox had bungled recruitment this summer, an assessment that seemed to be supported by Amad Diallo. Bruno Fernandes had a point in Como. Michael Carrick had picked the wrong tactics for the occasion. One of the most significant problems at Old Trafford is that the wrong executives, appointed by the wrong owners, are not exploiting the financial heft that United, even loaded with debt, still have. Another is that Carrick is not a good enough coach to paper over the cracks.

Those weren't the problems at Stamford Bridge on Saturday. This was a game lost for United by senior players. Fernandes and Amad, who is now 24 and has played over 100 games for the club, partly number among them. It is rarely wise to over-index on anyone missing chances; perhaps only Amad's last shot of the first half could reasonably have been termed one he should have scored. Then again, if you've got notes about tactics, you had best exploit the mismatches that come your way.

Whether through Chelsea's early disorganization or Carrick's adjustments -- which included center forward Bryan Mbeumo peeling off to the right and taking center backs with him -- Amad and Fernandes were afforded space and time to excel. Had they exploited them in the first half, United would have been firmly in the ascendancy.

Perhaps United heads would have melted anyway. It does not seem to take much to unleash a chain reaction of mental anguish on this team. One clumsy error begets two or three more, typified by Morgan Rogers' opener. Thirty percent individual brilliance, his clipped finish was as much a function of no one defending the space he was running into. Peter Bankes had the best view of proceedings as Andrey Santos went steaming in on fresh air.

"When you concede a goal it's never a good goal to concede. Morgan went through the middle of us. The game was in the balance, and to concede like that was," said Carrick, pausing as if catching himself before he said something he regretted. "Yeah it was a big moment for sure. I'm just looking forward to getting the boys ready for midweek now."

From there the task fell to Martinez to escort Chelsea across the finishing line. An arm on the midriff was not enough to slow Rogers' advance, so the next time their paths crossed, the Argentine went altogether more physical, rugby-tackling the attacker as he was making his way away from goal. It wasn't just that it was a clear yellow-card tackle; Martinez didn't even stop the attack.

It took two more hacks from Martinez and Diogo Dalot before the ball ran away from Rogers. The resulting free kick was cleared for a corner, at which the man they call The Butcher thought it was wiser to start carving up Wesley Fofana than defend the delivery into the box.

Martinez was the most obvious culprit, but right across the field United flatlined the moment Chelsea scored their first. Even the 13 minutes between Rogers' goal and the contest effectively ending with a Cole Palmer penalty saw a string of players lose the run of themselves. Carlos Baleba had hardly excelled beforehand, but passes he was clipping with a pitching wedge before were now being smacked around with a driver. United could not pass their way out of the pressure that Chelsea applied to them in their own half. Free kicks flew to no one in particular, although perhaps it shouldn't have been surprising that no one was connecting with balls in the air when all their heads were on Mars.

What follows will be the usual psychodrama of Manchester United, all the more so if results go against them and they find themselves in the bottom three at the end of the weekend. At the time Carrick was asked about it, that was the position United occupied, with Nottingham Forest drawing at Brentford. "You've got to keep moving forward and winning games, it's as simple as that. There's no words that make it any different. You've got to move forward and win football matches, it's as simple as that."

It does not look simple. Their nine-game winless run is United's longest since 1988. With games against Roma and Aston Villa to come, double figures seems a real risk. Carrick confirmed he will be in charge for the first of those games on Tuesday night, but the two-week sacking window that is a November international break looms large. And yet, if the United hierarchy has backed its manager after he did bungle the tactics against Como, how could his sacking be justified when his players took events out of the coach's control?

Carrick certainly had the backing of the traveling fans, who went through the full repertoire of chants against the Glazers, Sir Jim Ratcliffe, Wilcox and the new stadium. All those grievances are well merited, but this was only a game lost by the executives in the sense that they should long ago have dispensed with some of the underperformers, with or without the offer of a transfer fee.

There will be the next round of the familiar debates on ownership and on how long Carrick might last. All of those will start from what these players did wrong. They are a constant through line in the perma-crisis, garlanded with individual awards, bedecked with honors for their international side and chronically incapable of delivering to the standards that they demand of others at United.

#1137. Fleetwood knock out Arsenal in one of biggest shocks in League Cup history

Leaving Highbury was a wrench for Arsenal in 2006, but it was not the case 20 years later. They could not wait to get out of the stadium with the same name after a night that left Mikel Arteta looking haunted.

Fleetwood Town did not have any marble halls; they did not even have enough space in their car park for the three coaches carrying Arsenal’s entourage, but they have a proud tradition, spirit and, as a result, they will dine out on a result that will be celebrated for months and talked about for decades.

Eighty-four rungs separated these teams at kick-off, but, now and again, you get a situation when the floodlights are on, belief is high and the sense of history is prevalent. It is an intoxicating combination and, gloriously, the stars aligned. Mission impossible was completed.

Having chiselled out a 1-1 draw in 90 minutes in which Max Dowman was sent off, Fleetwood dispatched five nerveless spot-kicks, the last one thundered in by Conor Haughey after Bruno Guimarães’s penalty was saved by Jay Lynch.

“You have got to have confidence, haven’t you?” Haughey asked. “I just thought, I’m going to run up and smack it. It’s incredible. I come from Belfast and if you don’t have confidence, you will get eaten up.”

This was ignominious for Arsenal, an elimination from this tournament to rival the 1969 loss in the final to Swindon Town or the 2012 exit to Bradford, then also of League Two. What made this so astonishing was the fact that Mikel Arteta went so strong.

You should never be surprised by anything these days, but, even still, an eight-minute delay because of a drone flying over this wonderful little venue would not have been on anyone’s bingo card. The precaution was understandable. Only 10 days ago, one idiot escaped from a village to kick a rugby ball off the roof of an apartment block into the Gtech Community Stadium while Brentford and Liverpool were playing and could have caused serious injury.

So while the locals harrumphed as the players tried to keep themselves warm, no risk could be taken. Eventually, police apprehended the operator in a nearby park. It was something unfathomable, which was also true of what happened when the contest resumed.

The anticipation was that Arsenal would saunter clear against opponents who had lost at Exeter City on Saturday, leaving them 18th in England’s fourth tier. But it only took a few skirmishes to appreciate this was not going to be the cakewalk anticipated in what was the biggest occasion in Fleetwood’s history.

Arteta absolutely knew his team were not operating at the levels they should have been. He was wrapped up against the elements in a thick black jacket but, every so often, he would express his exasperation at Jurriën Timber, captain for the night, to “get forward!”

They were in a battle, that much was obvious, and one challenge from Shaun Rooney – so forceful you thought the ball might burst – sent Myles Lewis-Skelly spinning like a top. How Fleetwood’s fans loved it, roaring their approval as the young England international hit the ground with a thump.

Arsenal had one good chance when Dowman skipped down the right and dragged a shot across the box that Viktor Gyökeres could not divert but then, wonderfully, things took a totally unexpected turn when Fleetwood poked their noses in front.

It was a League Two goal in its simplicity, but that is no criticism. Harrison Neal helped a long ball forward, putting it behind Marli Salmon and Aaron Loupalo-Bi relished the chance to get into a foot race, grappling with the England Under-17 international.

Salmon looked like he had him at one point, but Loupalo-Bi was strong – not to mention composed – and he held off the challenge to slide a left-footed shot through the legs of Illan Meslier, who was making his Arsenal debut. What followed was unique to the magic of an English cup tie.

Bruno Guimaraes, Martin Odegaard, Kai Havertz and Eberechi Eze are among the players stepping off the bus, so at the very least it will be a strong bench.

Aside from their stadium being called Highbury, Fleetwood Town’s red shirts with white sleeves also bear a striking resemblance to Arsenal’s home kit. The club in its current guise was founded in 1997, although previous iterations date back to 1908 under the name Fleetwood FC.

There is no evidence or anecdote suggesting Arsenal were the inspiration, so it appears the kit clash is a coincidence. Arsenal will be wearing their navy away strip.

The club’s most famous son is surely Jamie Vardy, who scored 31 goals in 36 appearances for Fleetwood in the 2011-12 season before Leicester City made their move.

An unfamiliar opponent at a very familiar sounding venue, Arsenal play Fleetwood Town for the first time this evening at the Lancashire club’s Highbury Stadium.

Fleetwood, 18th in League Two, are the lowest-ranked team remaining in this season’s League Cup, having booked their place in the fourth round thanks to a victory at Sheffield United.

They were playing in English football’s sixth tier in 2009, and so while their stadium may share its name with Arsenal’s former home, the two clubs are worlds apart.

The League Cup is fourth of four competitions on Arsenal’s list of priorities, but Mikel Arteta should be able to rotate extensively while progressing to the quarter-finals. With a trip to Anfield on Sunday, that is a welcome luxury.

Kepa Arrizabalaga, Piero Hincapie, Cristhian Mosquera, Martin Zubimendi, Mikel Merino and Viktor Gyokeres are seasoned internationals in need of minutes and in line to start.

Max Dowman lit up Arsenal’s third-round victory at Ipswich Town, and 17-year-old centre-back Marli Salmon was not far behind him. Young striker and Northern Ireland international Ceadach O’Neill is also expected to be involved, and he may be joined by other academy players.

While attention is fixed on Premier League and Champions League success, Arsenal’s stinging defeat by Manchester City in last season’s final of this competition will not have been forgotten by Arteta or his players.

Matt Lawlor, Fleetwood’s manager, was full of praise for Arsenal in his pre-match press conference: “The champions are coming to town and they’re coming to our patch. The players need to be excited by it, not overawed by it. The respect is through the roof, but the fear can’t be through the roof.

“We’ve earned a game like this. We’ve had to go through round upon round of tough games, and none of them were easy. To get to where we are, we deserve that.”

Arteta has told his players that they must keep their standards high, with a lack of concentration or professionalism potentially their worst enemy against fourth-tier opposition.

Arteta said: “Our reputation, our pride, everything is in play. So every time you play a football match, and especially against a team in a different division, respect the game, respect every opponent because they deserve that, and then try to win and try to play a bit better than them.“We know the risk, and in football, things can get very equal the moment you are able to match certain things, and that’s why our basics and habits have to be through the roof to be able to win the game.”Full team news on the way shortly.

#1136. NWSL Decision Day storylines: Gotham, San Diego Wave chase Shield, last playoff spots up for grabs

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

There may still be a regular-season weekend left on the NWSL calendar, but for a few of the league's teams, Sunday's fixtures will see them slip into postseason mode a week in advance with plenty on the line on Decision Day.

The main characters will be Gotham FC and the Seattle Reign, each in control of their fate with different tasks ahead. Gotham have a chance to win the NWSL Shield for the very first time in Sunday's clash against the Utah Royals, with inconsistency in the final months of the season pushing the race for the trophy to the last day of the regular season. They are favored to collect the prize but have a formidable foe in the San Diego Wave, whose chances took a hit with last week's draw against the Boston Legacy.

The Reign, meanwhile, face the Orlando Pride in a game they must win to secure a spot in the playoffs. The North Carolina Courage are just two points behind them, and the Denver Summit three, with those two facing off against each other in the hope that the Reign slip up and hand one of them the chance to overtake.

Here's a look at what's to come as the NWSL regular season comes to a close.

Gotham have been favored to win the NWSL Shield for months, to the point that they had a seven-point lead in late summer. Even in a stretch of late-season ups and downs, though, their grip on first place has loosened but never slipped, leaving them well placed to win the trophy for the first time on Sunday. They boast a three-point lead over the Wave on Decision Day, a draw against the Royals enough to clinch the Shield, no matter what happens in the Wave's trip to Bay FC.

The bigger question for Gotham, though, is whether or not they will be at full strength a week before the playoffs begin. Jaedyn Shaw and Rose Lavelle both missed last week's 2-1 win at the Pride, while Shaw was also an unused substitute in a 1-0 loss at the Washington Spirit a week earlier. The pair have been Gotham's most impactful attackers this season, racking up a combined 22 goal contributions along the way; Shaw in particular has been both a goalscoring threat and a creative outlet, so much so that Gotham's attacking output fades considerably when she's not on the pitch. The league leaders might survive Sunday's clash without the U.S. women's national team standouts, the playoff-bound Royals set to enter the postseason with a middling defensive record.

Seven of the eight playoff spots are already booked, with three teams now vying for the final berth, and the margins will be tight for each of them. The Seattle Reign currently sit in eighth with 42 points, a win over the Pride enough to seal the deal. If they slip up, there are two teams in the waiting -- the North Carolina Courage and the Denver Summit, who play each other on Sunday. The Courage need to win and hope the Reign drop points to land in the top eight, while the Summit need to win plus a Reign loss to make the playoffs in their inaugural season.

There's a layer of unpredictability naturally baked into the scenario. The Reign not only have the easiest path -- win and they're in -- but they face a team whose playoff hopes were dashed some time ago. Their defense has really propped them up, conceding just 33 goals despite posting 39.96 expected goals against this season. Their rivals have their own strengths, the Summit finding form thanks to Lindsey Heaps' seven goals and three assists since her midseason arrival. The Courage, meanwhile, have this season's cheat code in Ashley Sanchez and speaking of...

With 20 goals this season, Sanchez's MVP argument writes itself at this point, but she has a chance to bolster her campaign on Sunday and make history along the way. She would set the NWSL's single-season goalscoring record if she scores against the Summit, while that goal or an assist would allow her to break Temwa Chawinga's single-season goal contributions record. It would be a worthy reward for Sanchez, whose conversion to left wing this season has been transformational and resulted in a well-earned return to the national team, thrusting her fully into the conversation for a spot on next summer's Women's World Cup roster. It is almost inconceivable, then, that her powers alone will not at least guarantee the Courage a spot in the postseason. Then again, they have maybe been overly reliant on Sanchez's form, the winger contributing to nearly half of the team's goals this campaign. They have been sunk, though, by a leaky defense, the Courage ranking in the league's bottom six for goals conceded. Missing the playoffs is unlikely to jeopardize Sanchez's MVP case, but it will speak to the Courage's limitations if they cannot sneak above the playoff line on the final day of the regular season.

#1130. NWSL Decision Day scores, playoff bracket, takeaways: Gotham FC cement their dynasty, Seattle Reign survive

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026 NWSL regular season might be over, but the fun is just getting started after an exciting NWSL Decision Day. All 16 NWSL clubs kicked off at once during a final afternoon of the regular season with plenty of high stakes on the line. This year's edition arrived with the NWSL Shield still up for grabs, awarded to the team with the most points, one final playoff spot in play, and multiple home-field advantages to settle.

When the final whistle sounded, it was Gotham FC that lifted the NWSL Shield, with San Diego Wave finishing just behind in second place, and Seattle Reign grabbing the final playoff spot.

Here are the big takeaways from the chaotic day:

Gotham FC 2, Utah Royals 0 San Diego Wave 1, Bay FC 0Kansas City Current 2, Racing Louisville 0 Washington Spirit 2, Chicago Stars 0 Seattle Reign 1, Orlando Pride 0Angel City 4, Boston Legacy 1 North Carolina Courage 1, Denver Summit 0 Portland Thorns 2, Houston Dash 0

With decision day done and dusted, the final results confirm the 2026 NWSL playoff bracket. More decision-day wins by Washington Spirit, 2-0 over Chicago, and Kansas City Current's 2-0 win against Racing Louisville confirm they get to host at least one home playoff game. First-place Gotham and second-place San Diego will also host, and if they win in the quarters, they will host semifinal fixtures.

San Diego, Angel City, and Kansas City all step into the playoffs on hot streaks. All three clubs are unbeaten in their last five games, with the Current on a five-game win streak.

NWSL playoffs begin Nov. 6, and the 2026 NWSL Championship will be played on Nov. 21. Fans can watch the biggest game of the year on CBS.

THE 2026 @NWSL PLAYOFFS ARE SET 🏆 pic.twitter.com/BtB3Wme9Uh

Friday, Nov. 6San Diego Wave vs. Utah Royals, 10 p.m.Saturday, Nov. 7KC Current vs. Angel City, 12 p.m.Sunday, Nov. 8Gotham FC vs. Seattle Reign, 12:30 p.m.Washington Spirit vs. Portland Thorns, 3 p.m.

Gotham needed only a draw to clinch their first-ever Shield in club history, but they did more than that and won 2-0 at home at Sports Illustrated Stadium. The club heads into the playoffs as the top seed after winning previous NWSL Championships as the lowest-ranked eighth seed.

The East Coast side has been a force to be reckoned with, winning the Shield during the longest season ever, the league's first 30-match schedule. The club had a significant points margin in late summer, but inconsistency and roster rotation due to injuries down the stretch pushed the Shield race to decision day, with Washington Spirit in contention through the penultimate matchweek and San Diego Wave still in contention on decision day.

San Diego did their part to make things interesting with a 1-0 win at Bay FC, but Gotham's early attacking surge set them up for success. Forward Midge Purce created the space for a laser cross in front of goal to Guro Reiten.

Gotham are making their Shield push 🏆Midge Purce sets up Guro Reiten as Gotham strike first on Decision Day 🤩🎥 @NWSL pic.twitter.com/8xLu5xuqKK

The lengthy season has affected all clubs this year, though Gotham's late-season string of injuries was particularly noticeable, with recent season-ending injuries to defender Bruninha and breakout rookie forward Jordynn Dudley. Attacker Jaedyn Shaw recently withdrew from U23 USWNT camps in mid-October due to an injury, and was available for Gotham's penultimate game last week but did not enter the match after warming up.

She's rocking a leg sleeve now and making an impact for the club, and scored the last goal after subbing in.

THAT’S JUST HOW IT’S DONE pic.twitter.com/BEj9KsAu6p

The goal sealed the win, and the return of Shaw and Rose Lavelle, both from injury, was a welcome sight for a team that has leaned on depth all season. Midfielder Jaelin Howell, among the team leaders in minutes played, left the match in the first half with a right ankle injury and will be evaluated closer to the quarterfinals. For now, Gotham capped the race that was theirs to win.

The eighth and final NWSL playoff spot came down to a battle between three clubs. Seattle Reign controlled their own fate, while North Carolina Courage and Denver Summit each needed to take the other out and root for Orlando Pride to win.

Seattle's identity this year has been more about organization and defense than goals, and their 1-0 victory over Orlando to clinch the final playoff spot was about as representative of the 2026 Seattle Reign as you could get. Playing particularly motivated, with playoffs at stake, and honoring longtime Reign veteran Jess Fishlock, Seattle pulled ahead just past the hour mark on a set piece that featured not one, but two flicks, and a clinical finish by center back Jordyn Bugg.

The backheel, the finish, just 🤩 pic.twitter.com/mtMSki9G25

#1129. Wesley Fofana’s Chelsea nightmare continues as Liverpool win shoot-out

Unfortunately for Chelsea, Wesley Fofana put his hand up twice. Firstly to concede the first-half penalty for handball that allowed Liverpool to equalise quickly after Chelsea themselves had scored from the spot.

And secondly to volunteer to take one of the penalties in the shoot-out. The defender had to score to keep Chelsea in it, but he woefully, nervously skied his effort high into a gleeful Kop and it was Liverpool who went through to the quarter-finals of the Carabao Cup.

LIVERPOOL ARE THROUGH TO THE QUARTER-FINALS OF THE CARABAO CUP! 🔴 Wesley Fofana blazes over to hand Liverpool their FIFTH consecutive victory ✅ https://t.co/M4n01R8DSk

There the reward for Andoni Iraola, the head coach, is a home tie against the club he left in the summer: Bournemouth. The draw has opened up for Liverpool, and they know it, with only Manchester City left of the other big guns. But despite again playing at Anfield, they would have preferred not to face such a dangerous and motivated opponent, who have just reeled off five wins and five clean sheets in a row under Iraola’s replacement, Marco Rose.

This was also a big win. A meaningful win. One that was celebrated as such with Dua Lipa’s One Kiss – an anthem on Jürgen Klopp’s run to Liverpool’s first Champions League final under him in 2018 – played over the loudspeakers at the end as the players joyfully milled around the pitch.

One kiss is all it takes 🎶 https://t.co/0jfujy4V94

“I am happy to feel it. We feel the support,” Iraola said when asked whether he sensed the momentum and togetherness building in his reshaped Liverpool side. It looks as though they are.

Fofana was Chelsea’s eighth taker, so they were running out of options, but it was a truly terrible effort. The 25-year-old turned and scratched his head – just as many Chelsea fans have done over his underwhelming, albeit injury-hit, contributions since his eyebrow-raising £75m move from Leicester City in 2022.

Both sides had the chance to win it earlier in the shoot-out. For Liverpool it was Kostas Tsimikas, who had taken the decisive kick to beat Chelsea in a shoot-out in the 2022 FA Cup final, but the Greek full-back also completely missed the target.

Tsimikas has the chance to put Liverpool through... And fires over the bar! 😱 https://t.co/eCKBT6njMB

Then Chelsea striker Emmanuel Emegha – on his debut – saw his kick saved, after an effort by Ryan Gravenberch had also been stopped. In the end, Liverpool’s stand-in captain Joe Gomez – still to score an actual goal – crashed in his kick before Fofana’s blunder. The 29-year-old Gomez finally “scored” and it was an assured strike.

This was the fifth penalty shoot-out between these two clubs, in all competitions, with Liverpool having now triumphed in all five. They won the toss for this one and elected to take the kicks in front of the Kop, which roared its satisfaction and did its best to unsettle the Chelsea takers.

Both stand-in goalkeepers – Giorgi Mamardashvili and Mike Penders – made one outstanding save each in the shoot-out. Chelsea substitute Valentín Barco was the other player to miss, hitting a post.

Chelsea blink first in the shootout! 🔵 Valentín Barco's penalty bounces off the post... https://t.co/rSXGfQctbI

The other efforts, in truth, were outstanding and assured with Liverpool, undoubtedly, benefitting from Iraola turning to his bench and bringing on Alexander Isak, Alexis Mac Allister, Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola. All scored their penalties.

Among Chelsea’s scorers was Jordan Henderson and the former Liverpool captain received a strange homecoming in his first appearance at Anfield for three years. He was booed, in the first half at least, and especially when he tucked the ball under his arm before Chelsea took their penalty – in normal time – which gave them the lead. Henderson turned to the stands, grinning.

Morgan Rogers buries the spotkick! ⚽️ Chelsea take the lead at Anfield 🔵 https://t.co/YlDn2gakRi

In truth it was more pantomime than meaningful and Henderson, like another former, Champions League-winning Liverpool midfielder Xabi Alonso – now Chelsea’s head coach – did not celebrate as Morgan Rogers scored. The penalty came after a rash challenge by Gravenberch, who crashed into Moisés Caicedo as the Chelsea captain ran on to Malo Gusto’s shrewd reverse pass inside the area.

Afterwards, Alonso faced more questions about his decision not to use Estêvão Willian. Despite injury to João Pedro and Cole Palmer’s suspension, there was only a place on the Chelsea bench for the 19-year-old Brazilian. And he stayed there even though Alonso used all five substitutions. Estêvão has made just two starts under Alonso, both in this competition. “The season is long and there will be moments for everyone,” Alonso said.

It was hardly a ringing endorsement especially as Alonso brought on Emegha instead. The 23-year-old striker’s contributions amounted to having his shoot-out penalty saved and then bizarrely and violently charging at Virgil van Dijk – his fellow Dutchman, is there an issue there? – long after the ball had gone, pushing the Liverpool captain over.

Virgil van Dijk was NOT HAPPY with Emmanuel Emegha 😒 https://t.co/UEtoJ7n5va

Alonso said the exit was a “small set-back,” and maybe it was, even if he started with a stronger side than Iraola. But with Chelsea not in European competition and unlikely to win the Premier League, it means he is already down to the FA Cup should silverware be won this season.

There is no VAR at this stage of the competition but referee Darren England appeared to get all the big calls right. Rogers claimed a penalty before Chelsea’s one was awarded, but Ronald Araújo was probably just too strong.

Morgan Rogers wants a penalty but he won't be getting one 🙅‍♂️ The referee waves it away and there's no VAR to step in... https://t.co/VR6yhBrx0I

And Liverpool’s penalty? Just what was Fofana thinking? Only three minutes after the lead was gained, Chelsea relinquished it as Van Dijk rose to win a header and Fofana had his arm outstretched. The ball struck it and Cody Gakpo beat Penders from the spot.

SEVEN League Cup games at Anfield - EIGHT goals for the Dutchman 👏 Cody Gakpo is the Carabao Cup king 👑 https://t.co/KaysZedwYr

Little did we know then it would be the first of 17 penalties, 12 of them successful, in front of the Kop with the last being Fofana’s.

"We are really happy with the performance!" Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola on his side's win over Chelsea in the Carabao Cup 👏 https://t.co/kW9DFXG5Iy

🗣️ "I had this paper but everything was wrong" 😆 Giorgi Mamardashvili's penalty notes weren't very helpful but that didn't stop the Georgian becoming Liverpool's shootout hero 🇬🇪 https://t.co/ckU9TOJoY3

🗣️ "[Gomez] was very confident, he was ready to shoot in the first five and I knew he was going to score" 😁 Andoni Iraola on Joe Gomez, Mamardashvili and Liverpool's newer players. 🎙️ @gabrielclarke05 https://t.co/mNLkTbCpOw

🗣️ "We want to show that fight and grit. It's mentality and I think that's what we're known for" 💪 Joe Gomez after Liverpool's victory over Chelsea in the Carabao Cup 🎙️ @gabrielclarke05 https://t.co/fjrbXp0L96

We are just getting under way to find out the four ties in the quarter-finals.

BradfordFleetwoodManchester CityBournemouthCrystal PalaceSunderlandLiverpool
