Fofana blazes into The Kop and Liverpool take their place in the League Cup quarter-finals. Liverpool have now won all five shootouts against Chelsea.

Liverpool beat Chelsea on penalties to reach the Carabao Cup quarter-finals! 🔴 https://t.co/pnCYwRrYzi

The Englishman has never scored a senior goal for Liverpool but emphatically smashes this into the top right corner.

Mamardashvili guesses correctly and makes the save to his right.

Penders makes the save and Chelsea, who now have the chance to go through.

The Englishman lifts it high into the net and we go on.

An emphatic penalty from the Frenchman right into the top left corner.

The former Liverpool captain has to score and he does, sending it down the middle. To sudden death we go...

The Greek defender has a chance to seal Liverpool’s place in the final eight but sends it over the bar.

The Argentine strikes the left post and Liverpool will have the chance to book their place in the quarter-finals with their next penalty.

The German makes no mistake, sending Penders the wrong way and putting it into the bottom right corner.

The Belgian calmly steps up and sends Mamardashvili the wrong way, putting into the right corner of the net.

The Dutchman scored Liverpool’s equaliser from the spot and smashes this one into the bottom left corner, with Penders going the wrong way.

He scored during the game and finds the net again. Mamardashvili goes the right way but the penalty from Rogers is very good, going right into the bottom left corner.

Again, Penders guesses the right way but, like Mac Allister, Isak lifts it brilliantly into the top of the net.

The Portuguese finds the net and we are all square after one penalty each.

Penders went the right way but Mac Allister lifts it over the Chelsea keeper.

They will be taken at The Kop. Chelsea goalkeeper Penders disappeared down the tunnel after the full-time whistle and re-emerges with a towel, potentially some penalty-saving notes as well?

Liverpool will take first and it will be Mac Allister who steps up first...

The final whistle is blown so we go to penalties at Anfield.

Looks like we are heading for penalties and if you are looking for omens... Liverpool and Chelsea have had four shootouts in the past: Liverpool won them all - the 2007 Champions League semi-final, the 2019 European Super Cup final, the 2022 League Cup final and the 2022 FA Cup Final.

A word on VAR (again). Watching this competition without the presence of the joy-killing invention is liberating. An occassional decision might get missed but, in the long term, you could live with that if meant you didn’t hear the words “it’s being checked by Stockley Park”. The decision just before, when Florian Wirtz’s shot touched Levi Colwill’s hand, was a case in point. It wasn’t a penalty but VAR being brought into play might convince you it was. Let’s get rid of it, please.

Double change for Liverpool as Isak and Mac Allister replace Ngumoha and Nyoni.

Huge double block from Chelsea and how have Liverpool not scored? Tsimikas’ cross to the back post is headed back across the six-yard box to find Wirtz, who you think is going to score but Colwill makes the block. Then Barcola has a shot blocked by Acheampong.

It is full time at both Craven Cottage and the Stadium of Light, where Crystal Palace and Sunderland have booked their places in the League Cup quarter-finals.

Tsimikas gives it away inside his own half and Chelsea counter. Neto drives inside and finds Rogers, who skips past Gomez. Rogers then finds the overlapping Palestra on the left side of the box and the Italian is denied by Mamardashvili at his near post.

Manchester City have just beaten Brighton 4-3 on penalties whilst on the south coast Bournemouth have comfortably beaten Aston Villa 3-0. Both sides are into the hat for tonight’s quarter-final draw.

Lavia cynically brings down Ngumoha as the Liverpool forward drove through the Chelsea half and is correctly booked.

Liverpool are taking off Van Dijk and Jacquet is coming on in his place. No injury for Van Dijk.

What a terrific cup tie this has been. It helps when there is an edge between the sides and you can feel the tension in the air. What has been noticeable in the last three games at Anfield, though, is the change in the atmosphere. Slowly but surely the locals are buying into what Andoni Iraola is trying to achieve. Liverpool could lose this game tonight by going all out to win it but there is a clearly identity developing that makes you think they are starting to get on the right lines.

After Gakpo fouls Lavia, Chelsea have a free-kick just over 25 yards out. Rogers lines it up but his effort is terrible, flying into The Kop.

Chelsea are going to make a triple change. Palestra, Barco and Emegha come on, with the latter on for his Chelsea debut. Gusto, Caicedo and Welbeck head off.

Good save from Penders. The ball comes to Barcola outside the Chelsea penalty area. The Frenchman drives inside before getting his shot away from the edge of the box. The shot takes a small deflection and Penders does well to make the save down to his left.

The game between Manchester City and Brighton at The Etihad has ended 2-2, therefore it has now gone to penalties.

Chances at both ends. Gomez whips in a cross from the right and picks out Araujo in the centre of the box but the Uruguayan’s powerful header is straight at Penders. He probably should have scored.

Then Chelsea counter and Rogers is in acres of space. His shot from just outside the box takes a deflection and goes behind for a corner, which comes to nothing.

Gusto’s behaviour in recent minutes has been appalling. First he went down after virtually no contact from Van Dijk and now goes down again, once more not a foul. He shows his boot to the linesman as if it came off in a challenge from Barcola but the replays show that his boot did not come off and he was attempting to con the officials.

Andoni Iraola is turning to his bench for the first time tonight and makes a double substitution as Wirtz and Barcola replace McConnell and Koumas. Some double change that for Liverpool!

Fascinating to watchg Trey Nyoni and the responsibility he has taken on his shoulders. He’s only 19 but those who have worked with him since he arrived at Liverpool as a 16-year-old will tell you he has a maturity of someone in their mid-twenties. He has tried to get on the ball and play, he’s been strong when it’s been required and always been in the right place to get a foot in. He’s going to play a lot of games for Liverpool if he maintains this trajectory.

Achemapong scythes Ngumoha down as the latter cut inside and the former is correctly booked.

Down on the south coast, Bournemouth appear to be cruising into the quarter-finals as Alvaro Rodriguez has put them 3-0 up against Aston Villa.

Should Rogers have done better there? In fortuitous circumstances, he is played through but he does not show the conviction to drive towards the Liverpool penalty area. His touch lets him and the ball rolls through to Mamardashvili.

Moments later, Rogers forces Mamadrashvili into a save to his left and the Liverpool players are furious that a handball was not given. It clearly hit Rogers’ arm before he shot but Chelsea do have the corner. Chelsea play it short before eventually Henderson swings it in before Araujo heads away.

We are back under way at Anfield. No changes from either side at the break.

Manchester City have equalised at home against Brighton, with Rayan Cherki’s free-kick from just outside the box taking a big deflection off his teammate Vitor Reis and ending up in the back ot the Brighton net.

Manchester City 1 Brighton 2 (70’)Bournemouth 2 Aston Villa 0 (58’)Fulham 0 Crystal Palace 1 (56’)Sunderland 3 Brentford 1 (56’)Liverpool 1 Chelsea 1 HT

Bournemouth have doubled their advantage against Aston Villa through Lewis Cook just over five minutes into the second half.

Possession: Liverpool 50%-50% ChelseaShots: 6-2Shots on target: 2-1Corners: 5-0Touches in opposition box: 5-9

The first half is brought to an end at Anfield and the game is level at 1-1 going into the break. Rogers put Chelsea in front from the spot only for Gakpo to also score a penalty moments later to equalise for Liverpool.

The outswinging corner is sent in from the left but Araujo’s header goes over the bar. Meanwhile, Lacroix is slowly limping his way around the pitch to the tunnel and is moving very gingerly, which could suggest an extended period on the sidelines.

As we enter three minutes of added time, Colwill replaces the injured Lacroix.

Liverpool can sense a second goal. First, Gakpo has a shot saved by Penders before Ngumoha wins the hosts a corner. Before that is taken, play has been stopped as Lacroix is down clutching at his left hamstring.

Not a murmur from Xabi Alonso as his side take the lead. The penalty Morgan Rogers dispatched went in the same corner as Alonso picked in the 2007 Champions League semi-final and perhaps he had a sense of what was coming as Liverpool are now level and it’s a fair reflection of how an intriguing opening 45 minutes has played out. It really wouldn’t be a surprise if we need spot-kicks to separate these teams at 90 minutes.

Like Rogers moments ago, Gakpo sends the goalkeeper the wrong way and puts the penalty away to equalise. Gakpo slots into the bottom left corner in front of The Kop and the Dutchman continues his fine scoring record in this competition. Both sides have been gifted penalties and both teams take advantage.

Cody Gakpo slots home a penalty to equalise for Liverpool against Chelsea! 💪 https://t.co/rS775LH0Gb

Like London buses, two penalties come in quick succession. From a Liverpool corner out on the left, Fofana is penalised for a handball and the referee has no choice but to point to the spot. The Chelsea players protest but it clearly hit Fofana’s arm, which was above his head.

Rogers sends Mamardashvili the wrong way and puts Chelsea 1-0 up in front of their travelling supporters. It was a quality penalty from Rogers, who deposited it into the right corner of the goal. It is a gift for Chelsea, who did not look like scoring but are gifted a chance to score through that silly Gravenberch challenge.

Morgan Rogers puts Chelsea in front against Liverpool from the spot! 🎯 https://t.co/ocMXFNCW9F

Caicedo goes down inside the Liverpool penalty area and the referee points to the spot. It is a silly and needless challenge from Gravenberch, who slides into the back of Caicedo and gives the referee no choice but to give a penalty. Not that it would be overturned but there is no VAR anyway.

Ex-Liverpool man Henderson was holding the ball for a while but now hands over to Rogers to take...

They are into the second half at Manchester and Brighton have retaken the lead through Georginio Rutter. Brighton now lead Manchester City 2-1.

That is a gift from Chelsea. The communication at the back between Gusto and Fofana is poor, with the former playing a poor pass backwards looking for Fofana, who cannot reach it and the ball rolls behind for the easiest of corners for Liverpool in front of The Kop.

Gakpo takes an outswinging corner but Welbeck is on hand to head away at the front post.

We are yet to see the first goal of the night at Anfield but they are flying in at the Stadium of Light. Brentford have pulled a goal back against Sunderland through Callum Wilson and it is now 3-1 in the north east.

Chelsea want a penalty. Rogers goes down inside the Liverpool penalty area under a challenge from Araujo but it was a fair shoulder-to-shoulder challenge and that is not a penalty.

At the Stadium of Light, Sunderland are in dreamland. Malick Fofana has put them 3-0 up against Brentford closing in on half-time.

A wasted free kick from Chelsea, and goodness, Austin McPhee is not happy. Chelsea’s set piece coach was up on the touchline, remonstrating to nobody in particular but it was obvious to see the frustration that the plan he has worked on - a chip to the side, a cutback into the middle - has fallen down at the first attempt. To compound his fury, McPhee just blew a gasket after Chelsea were not awarded a penalty following a coming together between Ronald Araujo and Morgan Rogers.

Tsimikas has let Ngumoha down there. Ngumoha does brilliantly to dribble through two Chelsea defenders around the halfway line and drives down the left. He then plays the ball outside to Tsimikas, who should do so much better with his cross but picks out the front-post defender Lacroix.

Meanwhile at Craven Cottage, Crystal Palace have taken the lead at Fulham thanks to Eddie Nketiah.

McConnell becomes the second Liverpool player to be booked tonight for handball. He lost the ball on halfway and cynically handled the ball as Rogers attempted to counter. A fairly clear-cut booking for McConnell there.

A reminder that there is no VAR tonight and if the game is level after 90 minutes, we will go straight to penalties. Referee Darren England has summoned Chelsea captain Caicedo and former Liverpool midfielder Henderson over for a word.

Caicedo puts Tsimikas’ cross from the left behind for the first corner of the night. Gakpo sends in the inswinger but the whistle goes as Chelsea are awarded a free-kick for a foul from Tsimikas on Gusto.

There has yet to be a goal at Anfield but at the Stadium of Light Sunderland have doubled their lead over Brentford courtesy of Tymur Tutierov’s goal.

The first booking of the night at Anfield goes the way of the home side. Koumas slides in to try and block a clearance from Lacroix and is booked. Koumas barely touched Lacroix and that is never a yellow card.

Meanwhile, in the north east, Sunderland have taken the lead against Brentford through Chemsdine Talbi.

Brighton had led in Manchester but the home side have just equalised. Mateo Kovacic has scored from range to bring Manchester City level with five minutes to go in the first half.

Clear to see in these early exchanges that Cody Gakpo has been deployed as Liverpool’s main “striker” with Lewis Koumas, James McConnell - who played in the 2024 final when Liverpool beat Chelsea 1-0 - and Rio Ngumoha operating in behind him. Jordan Henderson seems to be the man whom Xabi Alonso wants to trigger Chelsea’s press. They are playing a rigid 4-5-1 formation but, this being Alonso, the system is always flexible. His ethos is to be able to play two or three systems in a game if needed.

Ngumoha drives at Neto down Liverpool’s left and is felled by the Portuguese forward. It is an obvious free-kick and Neto is a touch fortunate not to be booked for that blatant foul. Ngumoha, who was fantastic for Liverpool against Villarreal in the Champions League just over a week ago, already into the action.

Tsimikas clips in the delivery but it is headed away by Lacroix.

The second goal in the League Cup this evening has come in Manchester and has gone the way of the away side. Malick Yalcouye has put Brighton in front against Manchester City on the half-hour mark.

We are under way at Anfield. Who will book their place in the League Cup quarter-finals; Liverpool or Chelsea?

Jordan Henderson is busily going around geeing up Chelsea’s players, in exactly the same fashion as he did when he played in this stadium for 12 years. He got an ovation here in May, when Brentford drew 1-1, that left him extremely emotional but it remains to be seen what will happen when he gets his first touch this evening. There has been no acknowledgement - yet - from The Kop and the same is true for Xabi Alonso. But, then again, why would there be when there is such lingering enmity between these clubs?

Both sides emerge from the tunnel and we are just moments away from kick-off at Anfield. Here is a reminder of how the two sides line up this evening:

Liverpool: Mamardashvili; Araujo, Gomez, Van Dijk, Tsimikas; McConnell, Nyoni; Ngumoha, Gravenberch, Gakpo; KoumasSubstitutes: Alisson, Endo, Jacquet, Wirtz, Isak, Mac Allister, Chiesa, Barcola, Chambers.

Chelsea: Penders; Acheampong, Lacroix, Fofana, Gusto, Caicedo, Lavia, Henderson, Neto, Welbeck, Rogers.Substitutes: Sharman-Lowe, Colwill, Subuloye, Palestra, Barco, Nicoll-Jazuli, Estevao, Quenda, Emegha.

Has come on the south coast, where Bournemouth have taken the lead against Aston Villa courtesy of Amine Adli’s goal inside the opening 10 minutes.

“The cups are important for us this year. For sure, we face today a good challenge, coming to Anfield, and we want to be in the next round. It is another competition. We know it is another format, it is make-or-break, so we want to make it happen today with a great performance.

“From the beginning we have taken it seriously. We have a tough game and we want to have a good feeling that we are competing. We have to do many great things. In one game there can be many little games with the energy created. These players have played here before. We have practiced penalties but sometimes it is about the feeling of the day.”

The games at the Vitality Stadium, Craven Cottage and the Stadium of Light have just begun. That means four of the five ties tonight have started, with just the game at Anfield to begin in just over 10 minutes.

At The Etihad, Manchester City have kicked off against Brighton. Then, there are three 7.45pm kick-offs before Liverpool begin against Chelsea at Anfield at 8pm.

"I have trust that they can perform well" Andoni Iraola on giving youth a chance in his Liverpool side to face Chelsea 🔴 https://t.co/5Z9xoGgqHz

More than two years have passed since Rio Ngumoha chose to leave Chelsea for Liverpool, but the frustration remains at Stamford Bridge. The pain of losing a player of Ngumoha’s potential does not pass quickly, especially as the winger was part of Chelsea’s academy system for eight years. It must sting to see a London boy, one of their own, now delighting the Anfield crowd.

For many at Chelsea, the anger at Ngumoha’s departure in 2024 will probably never subside. Or, at least, it will not subside while he continues to develop so thrillingly at Liverpool. Such was Chelsea’s annoyance at the time of his exit, Telegraph Sport reported last year, Liverpool’s scouts were subsequently banned from attending matches at their academy centre.

Xabi Alonso spent five years as a player at Anfield between 2004 and 2009. He has returned twice as an opposition manager, with both ending in defeats; one as Bayer Leverkusen boss and one as Real Madrid manager.

All five games this evening are all-Premier League ties:

Manchester City vs Brighton 7.30pmBournemouth vs Aston Villa 7.45pmFulham vs Crystal Palace 7.45pmSunderland vs Brentford 7.45pmLiverpool vs Chelsea 8pm

The two sides already into the hat for the quarter-finals are Bradford and Fleetwood, who knocked Arsenal out last night. The draw for the quarter-finals will take place after tonight’s matches.

Tonight's Blues. ✊💙 #CFC | #CarabaoCup https://t.co/Q7pTQHkgDc

Come on you Reds ✊🔴 https://t.co/o9Rc2yjV7c

It is an all-Premier League tie at Anfield as Liverpool host Chelsea in the last 16 of the League Cup, with a place in the quarter-finals at stake. This will be the first managerial meeting between childhood friends Andoni Iraola and Xabi Alonso.

Liverpool beat Tottenham 3-1 at Anfield in the last round of this competition, which included a stunning goal from Dominik Szoboszlai to seal progression to the last 16. They earned their first home Premier League win of the season on the weekend as they beat Brighton 2-0. Iraola’s men come into this game off the back of four straight wins in all competitions.

“There will definitely be changes, but we want to win the game and we want to be competitive,” Iraola said ahead of this tie. “We have to see how the legs; we are not just in the Carabao Cup, but also in the Champions League and we have been trying to make changes from game to game. We want to be in the next round. We have been unlucky in the draw, playing Chelsea, and they have been unlucky also. But we want to be in the draw again and that only happens if you win. We need to rotate, all the top teams need to rotate when you are playing every three days. Sometimes you are forced to rotate due to injury or sometimes different demands in different games tactically. I am happy that everyone is involved. When we have had to use someone who has not played a lot of games, they have helped us. The more players we have in a good place, the easier my selection will be, even if it is hard to leave players out.”

Giovanni Leoni, Conor Bradley and Hugo Ekitike remain long-term absentees for the hosts with Jeremie Frimpong also missing. Florian Wirtz could feature despite going off with an ankle knock during the win over Brighton.

Like Liverpool, Chelsea also had an all-Premier League tie in the third round of this competition, beating Leeds 6-3 in a high-scoring affair at Stamford Bridge. Chelsea come into tonight’s game off the back of a 2-0 defeat against Tottenham in the league last weekend. Not only did they lose on Saturday but to make matters worse for them Cole Palmer was sent off. As a result of that red card, Palmer is suspended for tonight’s tie.

“We [Alonso and Palmer] spoke and for sure he knows the mistake he made,” Alonso said. “Things that you can avoid. I hope that this is not going to be repeated. He is aware of that, he is mature and it was a mistake. He is in a good space, he connects very well socially with his teammates. They like him, they want Cole smiling, they want Cole having fun, enjoying his game because when we see that, he will have a better team. I will just ask you because he has got this very cool persona, you probably know his personality is very interesting.”

Former Liverpool midfielder and current Chelsea boss Alonso has lost his two games as a manager against Liverpool; a 4-0 defeat as Bayer Leverkusen boss and then a 1-0 loss when in charge of Real Madrid, with both taking place at Anfield. Alonso is not the only ex-Liverpool midfielder to return to Anfield tonight as their former captain Jordan Henderson is in the Chelsea squad for tonight. Joao Pedro has missed the trip to Anfield because of a thigh injury which could rule him out for a few weeks.

The Premier league fixture between these sides at Anfield ended in a 1-1 draw back in May. In that match, Arne Slot was in charge of Liverpool with Calum McFarlane in interim charge of Chelsea. Chelsea won the reverse fixture 2-1 at Stamford Bridge. Team news from Anfield to follow shortly.

#1126. NWSL Team of the Week: Sophia Wilson returns to Thorns with goals, Gotham FC players step up for NWSL Shield

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The regular season might be over in NWSL, but that just means the fun is just getting started with the 2026 NWSL playoffs right around the corner.

Decision Day crowned a new NWSL Shield winner with Gotham FC and clinched the eighth and final playoff spot with Seattle Reign, and in between, eight games all kicked off at the same time, and we saw plenty of standout performances. That means it's the perfect time to give out Attacking Third Team of the Week honors.

After weekly matches across the 2026 NWSL season, Attacking Third analysts select players, a head coach, and an honorary captain based on weekend performances. Here you can find a mix of stats and data, analysis from our pundits, and highlights you may have missed over the weekend. If you're keeping track of who earned past honors, check out our previous team of the week.

It's been a long year, and it's not quite over. With the playoffs starting on Friday, that means our team of the week honors will have a playoff feel to them and solely feature players competing in the postseason. Stay tuned for more coverage of the NWSL playoffs.

On Decision Day, you can only control what's in front of you, and while North Carolina will miss out on the 2026 NWSL playoffs, goalkeeper Kailen Sheridan did what she could to keep the team in the mix down to the final minute. Made four saves on 12 shots faced and earned a spot in the league record books as the third goalkeeper to reach 700 saves, joining Jane Campbell and Alyssa Naeher.

In elite company ✨Kailen Sheridan is the 3rd goalkeeper in NWSL history to reach 700 career regular-season saves! pic.twitter.com/ScxaO01TI4

There might not be a newly acquired player who fits in more seamlessly with Gotham FC than Guro Reiten this season. Joined the club in mid-April and is now an NWSL Shield winner after scoring the opening goal on Decision Day.

Organized structure and defense are staples of the Seattle Reign identity, and outside back Madison Curry gave everyone watching a reminder of that. Led the backline in tackles (three), clearances (three), and duels (12) in a cagey must-win game against Orlando Pride. The group clinched the eighth and final playoff spot, and if they want to shake up the postseason, their reliable defense will be a huge reason why.

If you've been paying attention at all this regular season, then it should come as no surprise that rookie Mimi Van Zanten is back on the team of the week. She scored her second goal of the season and led the team in clearances (four), interceptions (five), and tackles (eight).

MIMI VAN ZANTEN HAS THE FIRST GOAL ON DECISION DAY ‼️The @sandiegowavefc rookie keeps the Wave's shield hopes alive 🌊🎥 @NWSL pic.twitter.com/ZKyGEtsMd4

Mimi my goodness what a player 🔥 pic.twitter.com/J9maf9hSjz

Led the team in clearances (four), and duels (10), all while creating enough chaos on a set piece to force an own goal.

teamwork makes the dream work 🙂‍↕️💅 pic.twitter.com/vXBGeHMHwM

#1123. What to watch in UEFA Champions League: Michael Carrick's Manchester United future on the line

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The midway point of the Champions League phase is upon us, and already the pressure is beginning to build on some of the biggest clubs in Europe. For some -- the likes of Bayern Munich, Inter and Manchester City -- the coming days will be about scrabbling back up the table and establishing a grip on one of the coveted top eight berths.

Altogether more significant are those teams who might have to legitimately worry about whether they can reach the top 24. On current form Manchester United are certainly among them, and their home game against Roma threatens to be critical for the club's Champions League prospects. Perhaps the future of their manager too.

A little over a week ago it seemed only logical to log the remainder of Michael Carrick's time as Manchester United manager in hours. Back-to-back defeats to Como and Bournemouth, each by a three-goal margin, had the club hovering around the drop zone in both the Premier League and Champions League standings. Club captain Bruno Fernandes had openly questioned Carrick's tactics, fostering a greater sense of mutiny in the aftermath of center back Lisandro Martinez turning both barrels on those in charge of appointing the manager and signing players. Remarkably, Carrick endured, part-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the rest of the hierarchy concluding that the manager, who had led United to third last season, deserved time to right this listing ship. In many ways, events on Saturday vindicated that assessment. At Stamford Bridge the Red Devils had much the better of the first half, a coiled spring ready to blitz Chelsea on the counter. The only slight problem, one obviously out of Carrick's control, was that they did not put the ball in the net. Then the United midfield whooshed open like the doors of the Starship Enterprise to let Morgan Rogers score the opener, and everything adequate was undone in a 14-minute, Lisandro Martinez-authored head loss.

You can't really hold the manager responsible for that, not when so many coaches have tried and failed to quell United's appetite for self-destruction. Then again, it's not like you can sack the players midway through the season. If the situation gets perilous, there's not much you can do but start afresh in the dugout and hope against reason that Eddie Howe (or whoever else) can get through to this squad in a way his predecessors couldn't.

Right now you'd doubt that Manchester United are on the cusp of existential peril -- relegation to the Championship seems a long shot -- but they are at risk of being a few million worse off from their European campaign. Lose at home to Roma and they would have three points with half the league phase played. Still to play: Sporting and Villarreal away, RB Leipzig and Bayern Munich at home. That makes for a critical occasion against Roma, whose free-scoring attack must have been licking their lips on Saturday lunchtime. This has the makings of a brutal ending to a tenure that started with such promise.

Carrick sees things differently. "Perception is a funny thing," he said on Monday, insisting he does not feel like a coach with two games left to save his job. "You can make things look different ways and think about all sorts of different things. The commitment of the players to the club, to me, to each other - do not question at all. We need to play better, we can make better decisions, but the commitment is not a thing at all."

And yet, much as Carrick's perception of the group might quickly change, so could the game's view of why the United hierarchy stood by its man a week ago. Was the manager afforded faith for the long-term job or did his employers just conclude there was no sense in rushing a change ahead of a tricky three-game run before the international break? Fail to beat Roma and Aston Villa and we will surely find out.

Even in the aftermath of a derby defeat on Halloween night, it did not seem there was much cause for doom and gloom among the Inter ranks. A three-point deficit to league leaders Lazio is surely retrievable for the defending champions, and while they have only three points from their first three games, winning a man down against Shakhtar Donetsk eased any lingering sense of crisis about Champions League progression.

And yet the mood music emanating from the blue-and-black half of the San Siro paints a far more worrying picture. Head coach Cristian Chivu questioned the "approach and determination" of his side, senior center back Alessandro Bastoni spoke of an "inadequate" mentality and Nicolo Barella was the most damning of the lot. "We haven't had the right attitude since the start of the season, and it's a negative thing," he said, framing his side's struggles as being against tiredness as much as their opponents.

All of which might be something of an overreaction to Milan scoring three goals from five shots worth 0.57 expected goals in the first half at the weekend. Are there deep-seated problems with Inter or is this a team missing a host of senior players, among them Lautaro Martinez, whose absence at the weekend prompted Chivu to unsuccessfully experiment with Marcus Thuram as a lone striker?

Martinez will be missing for the trip to Feyenoord, but even without the captain, Bastoni, John Stones and Curtis Jones, there is the requisite quality in the Inter ranks to win well in Rotterdam (particularly if Chivu brings Federico Dimarco back into the XI). Whatever their attitude might be, it has not stopped them running up a supremely impressive 2.5 non-penalty expected goals per game. As for Europe, it would not have taken that many bounces going in a different direction for this team to have seven-plus points and be thinking about a return to the last 16. Without wishing to go too Leslie Nielsen about this, there really is nothing to see here.

Equally, when your players and coaches start talking in such apocalyptic terms, it is much more likely to bring on, well, the apocalypse. Or at least its Champions League league phase equivalent of an unseeded berth in the knockout playoffs/punishment round. That and some dropped points against Como and Atalanta.

Last time out we suggested that Arsenal's depth might hold the key against Bayern Munich late on and, like the stopped clock this column is, we were vindicated as Viktor Gyokeres turned provider for Declan Rice's late winner. Ultimately in the closing stages all Vincent Kompany had to turn to off the bench to aid his attack was a banged-up Luis Diaz and a faltering youngster in Lennart Karl. A fortnight later, even that would be an upgrade on the situation Bayern find themselves in as they travel to Madrid.

Saturday's 2-2 draw with Borussia Dortmund came at the cost of Ismael Saibari and Serge Gnabry, both of whom will be missing for some time yet. Jamal Musiala is also on the sidelines with a thigh injury and Diaz has only just returned to the field as he steps up his recovery from a hamstring injury. The best-case scenario for Bayern is that Michael Olise, who also exited early at the weekend, is able to play in some capacity, but director of sport Max Eberl described the Frenchman's situation as "day to day".

If Olise is not fit, it may be that the three attacking midfielders are Karl and two left backs, Alphonso Davies and Nathan Brown. It would take quite the center forward to knit all that together. A Ballon d'Or winner. Harry Kane's headline contribution to Der Klassiker might have been the missed penalty at 1-0, but the No. 9 ended this game with an assist for Dayot Upamecano and 0.43 expected assists total. Remarkably for a center forward, that was not even that far ahead of his season average of 0.32. That's 97th percentile for creation. It will not surprise you to know he ranks in the 99th percentile for shots and xG.

As Arsenal discovered to their cost in the last round of Champions League games, you can take away Kane's shooting chances, you can even take away his elite supporting cast, but he might still find a way to lay one on a plate for a teammate.

#1122. When humans disappear, biodiversity takes a surprising turn

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Emma Marris is a writer in Portland, Oregon.

Life-sized puppets in a remote village in Japan symbolize depopulation in the country. Credit: Buddhika Weerasinghe/Getty

Less than an hour’s train ride from central Tokyo, ecologist Kei Uchida walks through glades of mountain cherry trees and meadows filled with susuki grass as tall as an elephant. The researcher smiles when he spots something by the trail: a tangled orb of grass stalks, at about knee height. It is the nest of the tiny Eurasian harvest mouse (Micromys minutus), a species that has been on the decline in this area and has been targeted for protection.

Ecosystems depend on people: don’t abandon them

Ecosystems depend on people: don’t abandon them

Volunteers saved this location around Mount Tenran from development 30 years ago, and today they monitor its plants and animals, thin its forests and even plant and harvest rice — all in the name of biodiversity. Here, nature needs people. In the shallow water of the rice paddy, fish as small and arched as an eyebrow swim, and just above the water’s surface, dragonflies mate. At dusk, fireflies dance above the fields.

Uchida, an environmental scientist at Tokyo City University in Yokohama, and his colleagues included this site in a study of thousands of species in more than 150 wooded, agricultural and ‘peri-urban’ landscapes in Japan1. Unsurprisingly, they found that the diversity and abundance of most species declined at sites where the human population was growing. But they also found that biodiversity declined in places where the number of people was decreasing (see ‘Lost life’). This result — and others like it in different parts of the world — contradicts the common assumption that when people leave, nature always thrives.

Japan and many other nations are seeing a vast emptying of rural areas as people flock towards urban centres. Studies2 are showing that this can have a detrimental effect on biodiversity in the depopulated areas, which creates new challenges. Rather than simply setting up and managing protected areas, conservation officials must consider whether and how to recruit, train and support people to be permanent parts of some ecosystems.

I’ve joined Uchida and local volunteers to learn more about how human activity can increase biodiversity. Uchida says that this area is a typical satoyama landscape — a term that combines the words for village and mountain. “Agriculture and living things can coexist,” Uchida says. But Japan’s satoyama are being lost to depopulation and urbanization.

In this area near Mount Tenran, as in many woodlands across Japan, humans spent centuries cutting trees for fuel and removing fallen leaves for fertilizer. That opened up the forest and benefited specific plants and insects. But when that activity stopped, the forest became dense and closed in again. “We have used the woods for 1,000 years, but not lately,” Uchida says. Now, young students are being given small handsaws and taught the centuries-old art of woodland thinning.

Kojima Tsubasa, a volunteer nature monitor, shows me where he sits in the evenings to count fireflies. There are two types here: the smaller heike fireflies (Aquatica lateralis), which prefer rice fields; and the larger, brighter genji fireflies (Nipponoluciola cruciata), associated with running streams. “It’s rare to see both at once,” he says, proudly. Four days ago, Tsubasa says, he counted 60 fireflies at this paddy. Often, he is not alone. Japanese urbanites, yearning for the charm of the countryside, come here to watch the fireflies at dusk. But after the show, they get on the train and return to the brighter lights of Tokyo.

Most Japanese people now have to travel to see fireflies — whereas once the insect’s bright beauty was right outside their homes. It’s a trend seen the world over. As recently as 1950, nearly 40% of the global human population lived in the countryside. According to United Nations data, just 19% of the world’s 8.2 billion people now live in rural areas. The global rural population is expected to peak in the 2040s and decline thereafter.

In some countries, that rural decline is well under way. Japan’s total population shrank by four million between 2015 and 2025, and the rural population is shrinking even faster. In 2025, just 8.6% of its population was classified as rural. Peter Matanle, an independent environmental social scientist who worked with Uchida on the biodiversity study, calls Japan a “vanguard country” that other nations can learn from when it comes to depopulation. European Union data, for example, show that between 2015 and 2024, rural areas in Europe lost 0.2% of their population per year. Furthermore, rural communities tend to have older populations than do urban communities, a harbinger of further depopulation.

Uchida and his co-authors studied the effects of this demographic shift by examining data on 464 species of bird, butterfly, firefly and frog as well as nearly 3,000 plant species collected in various landscapes across Japan over periods of 5–17 years, starting in 2004. They found that biodiversity declined in areas where there was greater disruption of the landscape — either by people moving in and building infrastructure or by agricultural intensification, in which corporate farms replace smaller, family-run operations.

Rewilding the planet: how seven artificial islands could help a dying Dutch lake

Rewilding the planet: how seven artificial islands could help a dying Dutch lake

They also documented declines in biodiversity in places abandoned by people. Although that might seem paradoxical, the researchers note that when irrigation ceases, amphibians and many insects can no longer reproduce; other ecological niches are lost as well. The resulting dry, abandoned landscape is too fragmented for many species to recolonize. “Leaving it alone isn’t doing anyone any good,” Matanle says.

Similar relationships between rural depopulation and biodiversity have been documented in Europe. A study of 70 sites in Albania, Bulgaria, Croatia and Greece found that rural abandonment in these countries had “a consistent negative effect on bird communities”2. The species hit hardest were those that populate farmlands, according to the researchers. A European Commission monitoring scheme found that populations of farmland birds in Europe declined by 58% between 1980 and 2024, as agriculture intensified in some locations and moved out of others.

Birds are not the only organisms that have thrived in human landscapes. In Sweden, ‘semi-natural grasslands’, which have been cleared by humans and are kept open by livestock, are prime habitat for one-third of the country’s threatened species, and can contain up to 40 plant species per square metre3. As people left the countryside after the Second World War and land use evolved away from extensive pastures, the total area of these grasslands decreased by more than 90% in some regions4. In many cases, the removal of grazers led to the land being converted to row crops or forest — due to either spontaneous growth of trees or intentional planting for timber. Both types of forest are less biodiverse than the semi-natural grasslands they replaced.

In Spain, ecologist Francisco Lloret, at the Autonomous University of Barcelona, says that as people leave the countryside, biodiversity falls because some species are losing habitat and others are losing food. Vultures and other scavengers, for example, have relied on livestock for centuries, but that source of food is disappearing.

A revolution is sweeping Europe’s farms: can it save agriculture?

A revolution is sweeping Europe’s farms: can it save agriculture?

Wooded or herbaceous areas on the edges of fields are also in decline. In Mediterranean countries such as Spain, fields are often bounded by herbaceous borders — or by dry stone walls, which shelter many vertebrates and invertebrates. When such walls are knocked down to make larger fields for modern agricultural systems that require fewer people, those organisms are lost.

Why do so many species thrive in low-intensity farming landscapes? The mechanisms behind the relationship vary from species to species, say researchers. Some organisms prefer the standing water of rice fields, some tend towards the grasslands kept open by mowing or livestock, and some thrive at the edge of a forest. But the overarching themes of research seem to be that many species rely on the maintenance of a mosaic of habitat types and regular, modest disturbance through activities such as seasonal flooding, livestock grazing, burning, thinning and patchy clearing. Inhabited landscapes that experience such disruptions often host more species than a large expanse of undisturbed forest does.

These are the Arcadian landscapes of the Romantic poets, of The Wind in the Willows (1908) and of My Neighbor Totoro: culturally beloved ecosystems that have supported a suite of species since at least the Iron Age. “Biodiversity has evolved in the last millennia with people and human activities,” Lloret says. Some species might even have evolved to fit better into human landscapes. However, Lloret cautions that there are no universal rules. Context is king. In some places, depopulation increases biodiversity. Top predators, such as wolves, often do best in places without people. In the tropics — home to the most biodiverse places on Earth — few countries are experiencing depopulation and habitat loss is a much greater concern.

In response to biodiversity losses linked to rural depopulation, a team of conservation researchers in the Czech Republic and Poland have called for small-scale farming as a conservation tool to save farmland birds5. As a bonus, such farming communities would provide “high aesthetic and heritage values”, the team argues. Uchida and his colleagues suggest “a new interventionist wilding” to complement rewilding efforts that seek to set up nature to run itself. Some schemes run by the EU aim to support farmers and biodiversity, but they’ve been criticized as being ineffective6.

After my hike with the volunteers and Uchida, we emerge from the forest just as the sky opens and rain begins to pour. We go to a nearby bakery for a Japanese snack called curry bread, and I ask the question that has been on my mind all day: who will do the work of creating habitats for vulnerable species in the countryside in the future?

#1120. Everton give Burnham something to shout about by booking quarter-final spot

David Moyes took a glug of water and glanced up at the big screen away to his right, almost as if he wanted confirmation that what he was seeing was true.

Had he looked behind him, Moyes would have seen Andy Burnham and his wife, Marie-France, in raptures, along with thousands of others. It was true, all right. Everton had scored their third goal and were bounding into the Carabao Cup quarter-finals, seemingly without a care in the world.

What a happy change of direction. Moyes has spent months spinning plates, dealing with owners who do not care about a proud club and want to sell up and a squad that was left criminally short in the transfer window. Then, before Newcastle’s visit, came more disruption.

Jack Grealish’s selfish and reckless decision to go Awol from training on Monday could have been a catalyst for more misery and invited Newcastle to deliver a hammer blow to Everton’s season, but again, Moyes fostered a siege mentality. He was rewarded in the most emphatic fashion.

True, Newcastle collapsed like a deckchair without hinges and this performance – which encouraged many of their 8,000 followers to head for the exits early – would not have done anything to convince those who view Matthias Jaissle, the head coach, with ambivalence to change their minds.

The lack of discipline in their ranks was exposed when Dan Burn scored a late consolation and ended up in a melee with James Tarkowski and Joelinton. But the issues Jaissle, who lamented that “we must improve”, has to correct are for another day: this contest belonged to Everton.

Thierno Barry had provided the finish that secured a trip to Fleetwood in December and what an opportunity it is for Moyes to make Everton semi-finalists in this competition for the first time since 2016. Whether Grealish will have a part to play in it remains to be seen.

Thierno Barry with Everton's third! 🔵 https://t.co/dyb8fKud8N

The last thing Everton needed on a night of such importance was a distraction. Grealish will have a tough job mending relations, particularly with Moyes, but there was a paradox: though he had caused a major issue for 90 minutes he became an irrelevance.

Moyes is impatient to give Evertonians a big day out and his only focus was on crossing this hurdle – for all that Newcastle have had a turbulent start to the campaign, they are dangerous opponents and you wondered in the fraught opening 30 minutes if they might exacerbate the hosts’ woes.

As Jaissle hopped and squirmed on the sidelines, imploring Newcastle forward, chances came and went: Harvey Barnes had a header saved, Fabian Schar tested Jordan Pickford from 30 yards while Vitalii Mykolenko and James Tarkowski made huge goal-saving challenges.

“We should have scored more goals,” Jaissle, who was dressed as if auditioning for the role of The Milk Tray Man, growled. “It [losing] was shocking as the game was not that bad.”

Moyes was infuriated by Everton’s initial inertia, so much so there was a point when the Scot prevented Merlin Röhl, his own full-back, from taking a throw-in until Tarkowski and Jake O’Brien had complied with his gesturing to get 10 yards further forward.

It might have looked old-fashioned but it worked. Suddenly Everton started asking questions, Hayden Hackney almost got on the end of a cross from Mykolenko, and it encouraged the supporters on the vertiginous South Stand to raise their voices and become more involved.

What they needed was a goal to set things alight and in the 34th minute, it arrived. Tyrique George won possession by Newcastle’s corner flag, the ball dropped at Hackney’s feet and he instinctively ushered it on to James Garner, who whipped a right-footed drive beyond Lukáš Horníček.

James Garner puts Everton in front against Newcastle in the Carabao Cup! 🔵 https://t.co/TzponbWyGU

The roar that greeted it was a mix of elation and wonder, relief and desperation. The locals have grown weary of seeing nights with potential end in disappointment but here was the foothold they craved and the opportunity they were ready to seize. Soon the lead would be doubled.

Hackney would score the goal, converting a super Barry cross, but let us acknowledge the fabulous refereeing of Farai Hallam, who waved play on when he might have whistled for a foul on Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall. And how Everton took advantage.

Hayden Hackney doubles Everton's advantage! 🔵 https://t.co/VIY0Iln3nI

It must be said the officiating this week has, in the main, been outstanding. Watching a match without the persistent spectre of VAR has been liberating and you can see the referees have felt free to make decisions on instinct.

The whole experience of knowing a contest cannot be re-refereed has been better for all. It will not catch on, sadly, because too many people have gone too far down the road with VAR, but we should embrace the purity of “old school football” while we can.

Evertonians – the Prime Minister included – certainly embraced the buffer of a second goal and the fact Hackney scored it also felt like a throwback: a player who was plucked out of the Championship in the summer and encouraged by Moyes to show he could make the next step up.

He did that and so, too, did Everton, their progress was assured in the 69th minute when Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall dashed down the left and crossed for Barry to finish. Moyes puffed out his cheeks as it hit the net. He, more than most, deserved to enjoy this one.

#1116. Manchester United stun Roma with three-goal second-half Champions League comeback after dreadful start

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

If this feels like vindication for Manchester United, it shouldn't. The sort of unforgettable European night you could have been forgiven for thinking might be a long time in coming for this listing club, certainly. A fresh start to a season that seemed on the brink, perhaps. And yet everything else does not go out of the window just because this team made Old Trafford roar again in a thrilling comeback to beat Roma 3-2.

A modicum of the commitment, energy and application they showed in the second half and United would never have been in the hole they found themselves in in the first. It turned out that when United do not just throw in the towel on the concession of a goal, there's still a decent football team lurking in there. More significantly than that, there are players who are still committed to the cause and perhaps to the manager. It surprised many that Michael Carrick got the backing of those above him after the defeat to Bournemouth nine days ago. This was as clear an indication as any that his players share his commitment to the cause, the belief he articulated on Monday.

Carrick might, however, ask where exactly this had been on the many occasions adversity came United's way in the last month. Why has everyone not been playing with the ferocity that Matheus Cunha used to carry this team back from the brink? The Brazilian was so exceptional you could forgive the overexuberance of a late red card. It was the same quality that saw him force the penalty through which the petulant Bruno Fernandes halved the deficit. The equalizer was afforded to Cunha when Leonardo Balerdi cleared fresh air. The winner only required a helping hand from Shea Lacey, Cunha taking the ball to a narrow angle and rocketing in a goal that seemed unimaginable when the hosts were being booed to the dressing room at the interval.

Old Trafford had been electrified. It hadn't taken much, that penalty where Fernandes was lucky to get a second chance after a questionable encroachment call. When Bryan Mbeumo clipped both posts, it sounded like the wobbly roof might come off. All it had taken was a few minutes of intensity and a browbeaten crowd roared again. Hope can now spring at a ground that really wants to believe that Carrick can get this right.

And yet whether he can will remain in doubt when so many of his players can fail to execute a game plan for so long, as they did in defeat at Como last month. That much was apparent for Roma's first goal. It was evidently part of Carrick's tactical plan to get Diogo Dalot high up the field early in the move to apply pressure to the right wing back. Risky, given the threat Matias Soule posed at the other end, but a perfectly valid approach. What would be required is some willingness on the part of others to plug gaps if Roma turned the ball over at the right moment.

Make no mistake, Dalot, stood with gray shirts between him and the ball, was not really making himself available for the pass. When Roma turned the ball over, however, the left back did blitz it back into position. There was just no way for him to get back in time. For Fernandes, perhaps there were gaps he could plug. Kobbie Mainoo too could have got in position. Instead, the right half of the penalty area was wide open for Soule to collect a pass from Rodrigo Mora and drive past Senne Lammens.

This is the sort of goal that, once you have conceded once, you ought never to again. Strictly speaking, United didn't; it is just that the penalty they conceded five minutes later again came because no one was filling the space vacated by Dalot. This time Soule tried to turn provider before getting the ball back off a lackadaisical Harry Maguire clearance. His shot deflected off Ayden Heaven's arm, Donyell Malen doubling the lead from the penalty spot.

The 28 minutes that followed were perhaps even more troubling. The legends of this football club are forged in fighting spirit on European nights, and yet defeat seemed to be accepted. United did not manage to take a shot in the penalty area in the first half. Amad Diallo seemed to be the only man who could get the ball into those dangerous areas. Meanwhile Fernandes carped at Carlos Baleba over a pass he didn't like. Baleba gave it back too. United looked to be on the brink.

It speaks favorably of Carrick that he turned it around not through any obvious tactical adjustments but through getting his side to move the ball with a little more intensity. They delivered it, and at the club that Sir Alex Ferguson built, there will always be a belief that a manager can come back from the brink to reach footballing immortality.

And yet the common thread of recent weeks is not that United can be as good as they were in the second half but that they can consistently plumb the depths they hit in the first. It only takes Morgan Rogers running in a straight line, Nico Paz finding space or Leny Yoro slipping to begin a chain reaction of mental anguish. On the evidence of tonight, those momentary crises were never intractable. Doesn't that make it all the more infuriating that United players were the first to call it quits?

#1111. Mysterious anthrax outbreak kills hippos in Africa — raising concerns for human spread

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Rachel Fieldhouse is a reporter for Nature in Sydney, Australia.

Hippos in Virunga National Park in the Democratic Republic of the Congo have been affected by an anthrax outbreak over the past month.Credit: Evelyn Hockstein/MCT/Tribune News Service via Getty

An anthrax outbreak has killed at least 30 hippopotamuses in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) in the past month. No cases in people have been reported so far, but authorities say they are monitoring the situation closely.

The dead animals were first found in September in Virunga National Park in eastern DRC, and laboratory tests confirmed they died from anthrax, a serious infectious disease caused by the bacterium Bacillus anthracis.

The outbreak comes at the same time as health authorities and conservation groups in the DRC manage large outbreaks of Ebola and cholera, and the ongoing humanitarian challenges caused by armed conflict in the region. A disease outbreak of anthrax in wildlife puts further pressure on already limited resources, say researchers.

The anthrax bacterium is found naturally in soil worldwide and can infect livestock and wild animals if they encounter its spores. Officials at Virunga National Park said in a statement that teams have been monitoring the affected area and coordinating the safe handling and disposal of carcasses and there have been no new mortalities in the past two weeks.

David Hayman, a disease ecologist at Massey University in Palmerston North, New Zealand, says the main risk to people is from handling infected carcasses or consuming contaminated meat. The disease can be treated with antibiotics if caught early, but it can be fatal without treatment.

Although no cases have been reported in people during this outbreak, Charity Mutesi, an epidemiologist at the Uganda National Institute of Public Health in Kampala, says that infections can go undetected because people might decide to stay at home rather than going to a clinic for treatment. People often use herbs on the lesions caused by some anthrax infections, or might seek care from drug shops, private clinics or traditional healers, who do not report the cases to the national disease surveillance systems, she adds.

The DRC has experienced several anthrax outbreaks in animals and people over the past few years. In March 2025, an outbreak killed around 65 hippos. Fifteen people tested positive for the disease in bordering Uganda, two of whom died.

“It is very concerning that these outbreaks continue to happen,” says Ricardo Soares Magalhães, an epidemiologist at the University of Queensland in Brisbane, Australia.

#1106. Man Utd the masters of self-destruction as pressure piles on Carrick

So where do Manchester United go from here? It is never a good look when opposition fans start willing a rival club to stick with their manager, but that was the ignominy that had befallen Michael Carrick by the end of an afternoon in which Lisandro Martinez’s latest plastic hardman impression embodied the very worst of United’s self-sabotage.

After seeing their team go 2-0 up when Cole Palmer converted the penalty given away by Martinez’s lunacy, the Chelsea fans taunted Carrick with chants of “You’re getting sacked in the morning” and later “You’re going down with the City”, a nod to the other Manchester club who are crisis torn for very different reasons.

As the final whistle loomed, though, and with United just grateful Estevao had not punished Martinez’s red card more severely, the Chelsea fans had changed their tune. “Michael Carrick, we want you to stay,” came the chant from the Matthew Harding Stand and that cut far deeper.

And to think that the opening 45 minutes had offered United and their fans some hope of a little respite from the storm before ultimately giving way to an ever-darkening gloom.

Carrick, who had been given a stay of execution in midweek, said he still expected to be in charge for Roma’s visit to Old Trafford on Tuesday in the Champions League. But it is hard to escape the feeling that another managerial change will be coming at United before too long even if no one can be sure what happens next.

Equally, the prospect of more upheaval in the dugout might elicit little more than a shrug from fans pointing the finger squarely at the ownership and the executives they have appointed. The players were spared this time but Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazers remained the target of sustained abuse as did Jason Wilcox, the director of football.

Defeat here extended United’s winless run to nine matches, their worst sequence for 38 years. They have taken just four points from the last 21 on offer in the Premier League and seem to be sinking fast. Carrick was asked about the team becoming mired in a relegation battle. This is the territory United are in.

The strange thing is this could and probably should have been a day when they at least stopped the rot for a few days. But more non-existent defending and brainlessness from Martinez, who was sent off for planting an elbow in Wesley Fofana’s face, put paid to that in a second half in which Carrick admitted United “unravelled”.

Chelsea were cut open on at least five occasions in a see-saw first half and Matheus Cunha also had a goal disallowed for a narrow offside. Xabi Alonso’s side had opportunities of their own – you will always get them against this United team – but they were second best and lucky not to be behind. Everyone talks about United being there for the taking, but the truth is Chelsea, coming off the back of a miserable defeat to Spurs and Carabao Cup exit to Liverpool, were here.

The problem is Carrick’s team could not hit a barn door at the moment. They have scored just three goals in their last six league games and that lack of cutting edge was evident in the way Bruno Fernandes, back in the team as captain, and Amad Diallo (dangerous but with no end product) wasted excellent chances. That wastefulness would put pressure on any back line, let alone one with all the fortitude of wet cardboard. Chelsea were spared and exploited it with the help of the second and most corrosive acts of United’s self-mutilation.

We will come to Martinez’s sending off in a moment, but there had already been a cowardly act of a different kind from the Argentine defender before then in the lead-up to Chelsea’s opening goal soon after the restart.

By the end, with Estevao – making the most of a first league start of the season – running riot and Chelsea smelling blood, Carrick would have been relieved the scoreline was not worse. Michael Carrick said he expects to be in charge of Manchester United next week despite Lisandro Martinez’s moment of madness leaving the club mired in a relegation battle and on their worst run for 38 years.

United were urged to sell Martinez after the controversial Argentina defender was sent off for elbowing Wesley Fofana as Carrick accused his side of “unravelling” as they slumped to a 2-0 defeat at Chelsea.

It left United without a win in nine matches, their worst run since 1988, and at risk of being sucked into the relegation zone. They have won just two of 13 games this season.

The Old Trafford hierarchy gave Carrick a stay of execution in midweek and, when asked if he expected to still to be at the helm when United face Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday, the head coach replied: “Yes. I’m just looking forward to getting the boys ready for midweek now.”

Having been booked moments earlier for a foul on Morgan Rogers, Martinez was sent off for a second yellow. The incident came less than three weeks after the Argentinian was fined and publicly apologised for attacking United director of football Jason Wilcox and the board over transfer policy and was the latest in a series of mistakes from him on the pitch this season.

Joe Cole, the former Chelsea and England forward, believes United must get rid of Martinez.

“Whatever the next Manchester United looks like, Lisandro Martinez has run his course,’ Cole said on TNT Sports. “He’s at the scene of the crime too often for Manchester United and is at fault for moments and goals like that. So that’s probably his time done.”

Carrick refused to publicly criticise Martinez but admitted his dismissal was a “huge moment” and felt his team “unravelled” in the second period.

“Things have gone against us in a big way,” the United manager said. “It’s unravelled quickly. There’s a lot of emotion right now. It’s a huge moment in the game. Sometimes you get setbacks in games and you’ve got to deal with that better. I’ve not seen it [the Martinez incident] back so I don’t know if it was [a red card] or not. He’s gone to it and the referee gave that decision, but it’s a big moment.”

Asked if there would be a stigma attached to United potentially dropping into the relegation zone, Carrick added: “Not for me, no.”

And when asked how his players would deal with a relegation battle, Carrick added: “We’ve got to keep moving forward and winning games. There’s no words I’m going to explain to you now that makes any difference, it’s not going to change it. We’ve got to move forward and win matches.”

What do football fans actually want from their club owners? The model for most has been Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan and friends at Manchester City, owners whose hands are put frequently into pockets of unlimited depth, have made vast improvements to every aspect of the club and its community and are rarely ever seen, let alone heard from.

That view may have to evolve after certain verdicts about certain charges, but few envious glances from around the country have been cast towards the owners of Manchester’s other major club.

Manchester United’s accounts for last season suggest that ownership could be changing in the next three years, with a route to Sir Jim Ratcliffe assuming full control by 2029. But who would actually be the better custodians for United?

I’m good. It’s one of them – when you’ve had a result like we have, maybe a spell like we have, it definitely makes you hungry to push on and improve things. That’s what we have done this week.

We know it’s not been good enough. It’s obvious to say that. But it’s something we can flip and we are the ones who can control that. That’s the beauty of it for me. We are in control of it and know there’s something we can do about it.

I don’t need any assurances [from the board]. I totally understand what’s needed here. I’m just focused on winning games.

If there’s anything I take about beyond these four walls it’s how the supporters are thinking. That’s all that matters to me. I’m not interested [in external noise in the media etc], my only focus is on making us better.

[Do you think the players are behind you?] One hundred per cent, for sure.

Good morning and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Chelsea, who start the day in fifth, and 16th-placed Manchester United at Stamford Bridge. On Sunday and Monday it seemed certain that Michael Carrick would be relieved of his duties before today’s game but has survived for now, hoping to turn things around in the no man’s land that sometimes resembles a vote of confidence and at others a stay of execution.

Thirty years ago when Newcastle United were coming off the bridle in the title race with Manchester United, Alex Ferguson, as he then was, accused a Leeds team, who had been in freefall since the new year, of professional malpractice when they put in a rare display of passionate commitment and tenacity at Old Trafford in a 1-0 defeat.

“Why are they not in the top six?” asked Ferguson. “To me they’re cheating their manager. You wait and see the difference when they play Newcastle.” The hate between the Leeds and Manchester united fanbases was such, he implied, that they had decided to put a shift in because, for once, they feared the consequences if they had not. It seems to this observer that the boot is now on the other foot. These Manchester United players roused themselves to fight at Elland Road then chucked it in against Como and Bournemouth. If that’s not “cheating their manager”, what is?

Carrick will have to hope that some of the old hostility between Chelsea and Manchester United might encourage the players to run about a bit this afternoon and, at the very least, get stuck in rather than crumple spinelessly as they did last week. I doubt it would be enough to save Carrick’s job in the medium term but at least it would address whether they could stake a claim to be part of the rebuilding process.

As for Chelsea, who were awful in defeat by Brentford and Spurs either side of impressive victories over Bournemouth and at Everton, they need to find some defensive solidity, discipline and a way of terrorising defences in the absence of Joao Pedro. They are a work in progress still, in the fifth year of the hedge fund hegemony. For all that attacking talent and Moises Caicedo’s ability to steamroll midfielders, their defence does not inspire confidence and last year’s petulance continues to simmer.

Rooney added that his teammatesâ styles in the game often mirrored their personalities on the pitch.

âMichael Carrick was a little sneaky, calm one. Youâd be lying down hiding and suddenly hear a grenade bounce nearby â heâd thrown it," he said. "I was just all in, frontline of the trenches, straight in there."

So while Fergusonâs legendary leadership and the squadâs quality remain undisputed, Rooney insists that SOCOM and the PlayStation may just have played an underrated role in creating one of footballâs most dominant dynasties.

#1104. Barcelona's road back to the top runs through Lamine Yamal and Raphinha, and Aston Villa got a front row seat

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

There are normal ways to build up to a marquee UEFA Champions League match and there's Aston Villa, for whom the top searches under Google's news tab were all about being taken seriously. This was hardly an exercise in projecting confidence ahead of a trip to Barcelona; the club picked a fight with a broadcaster instead because, for some reason, they deemed he had the power "to stop our ascension in English and European football." Villa's year-over-year improvements are hard to deny, to the point that being somewhat competitive at the Camp Nou on Tuesday was not out of the question and they managed that much. There was just one problem, though.

Punching above your weight is easier said than done against this version of Barcelona.

Villa were no slouch but over the course of a 3-0 win on Matchday 4 of the Champions League, Barcelona were simply in cruise control. It is not that Villa did not pose a challenge – they sparked at times in the first half, Johan Manzambi responsible for the visitors' best chance of the game around the half-hour mark. There was simply nothing they could do at the Camp Nou, their ascension irrelevant even if it is true, because Barcelona are as close to the summit as it gets.

Barcelona barely put a foot wrong as they strung together a trademark performance, well-positioned to do the easy things when the time called for them. That was true as soon as the seventh minute when Joao Gomes, under very little pressure, played a perfect pass to Lamine Yamal with plenty of space in front of him. Even as a couple of Villa defenders tried to close the space near goal, Yamal found his crevice and finished the chance off. It was perhaps the easiest way for him to score his 14th Champions League goal, surpassing Kylian Mbappe as the teenager with the most goals in the competition.

Lamine stands alone 😤Yamal scores his 14th #UCL goal to become the competition’s all-time leading teenage goalscorer 👏Watch #UCL on @paramountplus 📺 pic.twitter.com/Va8Ks3SEHv

The hosts overwhelmed Villa's defense with ease, Yamal's goal merely the first sign of trouble for the visitors. Raphinha bagged a 12-minute brace in the second half, the entire collection of goals a remarkable example of defensive errors. There's a comedy to the Brazil international's first goal, something casual about his strike despite three Villa defenders in his vicinity, watching the ball as it flew into the back of the net. On his second, Joao Cancelo was essentially given permission to dance around Villa's defense to find a Raphinha that was virtually unmarked and converted again from close range.

Raphinha with a 12-minute brace 💥He has scored 19 goals for Barcelona this season in all competitions 💥 pic.twitter.com/R39J7g9y6M

The mistakes from Villa were glaring, almost obfuscating Barcelona's performance entirely. It was not simply a walk in the park, though – Hansi Flick's side got to roll out Plan A and showcase its strengths fully, the lopsided result reflecting the more subtle elements of their dominance. They were able to possess exactly as they wanted to, taking 16 shots and generating 1.99 expected goals along the way. Their attacking might is hardly a surprise now that Raphinha is several years into a career revitalization steered by Flick and now that Yamal is already well known as the sport's next great talent.

What was more impressive was their ability to completely shut Villa out, especially so considering the circumstances. The game state was not exactly a deterrent to Unai Emery's side – 10 days earlier, they let Manchester City have the ball and took their chances despite posting 0.61 expected goals and notched a 2-1 win in the process. Their total was a little better on Tuesday at Barcelona, generating 0.72 expected goals from nine shots, and this time they had the benefit of playing against an understaffed defense. A series of injuries have plagued Barcelona's back line in recent weeks, stripping a defense of the early season stability that had become a new trademark despite sticking true to the high line.

Villa, though, were unable to make much of a dent. Nicolas Jackson, who had eight goals in 12 games across all competitions before the trip to Barcelona, took just one shot on Tuesday. Any semblance of attacking threat never came through. Rodri was not exactly some great denier, either – the captain of Spain's World Cup-winning team only played the first 45 minutes, earning the right to exit the game early after another job well done. Barcelona ensured Villa were dull over the course of 90 minutes; the defensive mistakes from the visitors were the end product rather than the cause of the hosts' success.

On a day where Villa's ascension was cast aside, Barcelona's rise was hard to miss. The gap they are trying to make up is smaller and easier to envision but it does not mean that Flick's side does not carry a certain amount of baggage on each and every Champions League night. They are 11 years removed from the last time they won Europe's top title, a lengthy stretch for one of the game's most celebrated teams. Self-imposed financial hardship has hindered their progress but since Flick took the job two years ago, they have inched closer and closer to the winner's medals they have been eager to collect.

Beating Paris Saint-Germain, the undeniable favorites after back-to-back titles, to the podium is another question entirely, especially after a 4-2 loss in the French capital on Matchday 3. Flick, though, insisted that day was merely a step on the journey, an experience to learn from as they attempt to ascend up Europe's ranks themselves. Champions often make their case on difficult days and should Barcelona make a deep run, they will likely have the chance to do just that down the stretch. The road to the Champions League title, though, usually includes some impressively unfussy days and on Tuesday, Flick's side collected one.
